title: Andy Burnham says "We'll find a way to save Jodrell Bank"
author: Angela Ferguson
content:
![An aerial view at sunrise of the Lovell telescope at Jodrell Bank. Its huge white dish, taller than a house, is tilted upright on a steel cradle that sits on a circular track. Behind it, flat Cheshire farmland stretches to the horizon under a soft pink sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/937/cpsprodpb/62ff/live/6961bcf0-892e-11f1-b684-d3f861a1f4cf.png)
Jodrell Bank has lost its funding and is under threat of closure
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to save the UK's largest telescope at the Jodrell Bank Observatory.
The Lovell telescope, which has stood in Cheshire since 1957, is the world's third-largest steerable radio telescope.
But in July this year, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) said the site would not be prioritised for further funding after its current agreement ended in March 2028.
Burnham said: "Every one of my generation went on a school trip to Jodrell Bank, and there is no way that we can see its demise, and it won't happen under my government."
UKRI said its decision for the site was "the result of a comprehensive, evidence-based prioritisation process".
The Prime Minister spoke of his determination to save the site after being asked a question about its future in the House of Commons.
Congleton MP Sarah Russell, whose constituency includes the Jodrell Bank site, said it "is facing a significant problem in the medium term because of funding cuts".
She called on Burnham and No 10 North to work alongside her and Macclesfield MP Tim Roca to address the issue.
Burnham said: "I know there are changes that have been made in relation to research funding, but Jodrell Bank is a heritage asset for the country, as well as a research asset."
He said he would set up the meeting she requested, adding: "There must be a way to save Jodrell Bank, and I give a commitment today, at this despatch box, we will find it."
![A man in a suit and with glasses and short brown hair is speaking as he stands at the despatch box in the House of Commons. A woman with shoulder length red hair and a blue top sits on the bench to his right and a man wearing a dark blue suit and red tie is seated to his left. MPs can be seen seated in the row behind.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/c35f/live/ac6bbcf0-a637-11f1-8438-7134607e7611.jpg)
Speaking in the House of Commons earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said "there must be a way to save Jodrell Bank"
The Jodrell Bank site was first established in 1945 and pioneered radio astronomy and the study of galaxies beyond our own.
The site has also been immortalised in popular science fiction productions from the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy to Doctor Who.
Scientists have described the UKRI's decision as "heartbreaking" and "scientifically misguided".
More than 150 public figures have signed a letter calling for the government to reverse its decision and "find funding immediately to save Jodrell Bank".
Signatories include astronaut Tim Peake, musicians Sir Brian May, Johnny Marr and Jarvis Cocker, the bands New Order, Elbow and Doves and comedian Dara Ã Briain.
Scotland's Astronomer Royal Prof Catherine Heymans, physicists Prof Jim Al-Khalili and Prof Brian Cox, and Judy Spence, the daughter of the site's founder Sir Bernard Lovell, have also signed it.
All scientific observations at Jodrell are expected to cease on the 1 April 2028 unless alternative funding can be found.
![Johnny Marr, with a burgundy velvet jacket and black and white striped top, looks into the camera in front of the Lovell Telescope](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/8c5a/live/be7309b0-8f28-11f1-b5a8-c9ccaae98ebb.jpg)
Johnny Marr was one of several musicians to sign a letter objecting to the government's decision
The Lovell Telescope has a diameter of 250ft (76.2m) and is part of the e-Merlin array, a network of telescopes up and down the country that is operated by the University of Manchester from the site.
Jodrell Bank had a pioneering role in the development of radio astronomy.
Its work in tracking spacecraft in the early space race, and its research into quasars, pulsars and gravitational lenses, is also part of its outstanding scientific heritage.
The site has evidence of every stage of the history of radio astronomy, from its emergence as a new science in the 1940s through to the present day.
The Jodrell Bank Centre for Engagement is regarded as a separate entity and is currently not thought to be at risk as a result of the cuts.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to save the Jodrell Bank Observatory after UK Research and Innovation announced it would not prioritize the site for funding past March 2028. The facility, home to the Lovell telescope, faces potential closure and the cessation of scientific observations unless alternative funding is secured. Over 150 public figures, including scientists, musicians, and astronauts, have signed a letter urging the government to reverse the funding decision.
key_points: UK Research and Innovation decided not to prioritize Jodrell Bank for further funding after its current agreement ends in March 2028.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated in the House of Commons that his government will find a way to save the facility.
Scientific observations at Jodrell Bank are expected to cease on April 1, 2028, without alternative funding.
More than 150 public figures signed a letter calling for the government to secure immediate funding to save the observatory.

title: ’A giant leap forward’: Nasa launches powerful new space telescope - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
author: DM Editorial
content:
Wed, 02 Sep 2026
![dailymirror Logo](https://www.dailymirror.lk/assets/assets_new/images/logo-dm.png) 
![](https://www.dailymirror.lk/assets/assets_new/images/logo-dm.png) 
![](https://bmkltsly13vb.compat.objectstorage.ap-singapore-1.oraclecloud.com/cdn.sg.dailymirror.lk/assets/uploads/image_0a555246b0.jpg)
BBC - Nasa's powerful next-generation telescope has blasted off into space from its launchpad in Florida, with a mission to explore dark energy, black holes and other mysteries of the Universe.
The Nancy Grace Roman telescope will capture vast panoramic views of space, with a field of vision 100 times larger than both the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, Nasa says.
The mission begins with a 100-day journey to a vantage point roughly one million miles from Earth, where the telescope will then start charting planets outside our solar system, known as exoplanets.
"Roman is going to change the way we look at the Universe," said Nicky Fox, a Nasa administrator.
The successful launch of the telescope took place on Sunday morning local time from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
Jackie Townsend, a project manager on Nasa's Roman telescope, described it as "glorious" at a news conference afterwards. "The ride was magnificent. It put us right where we wanted to be."
About 30 minutes after launch, Roman separated from its SpaceX rocket and is now heading towards its orbiting point around a million miles away.
Fox said Roman "is going to discover tens of thousands, maybe even 100,000 new exoplanets" - referring to planets located outside of our solar system.
"Why do we care so much about exoplanets? Because one of our main goals at Nasa is answering the question, 'Are we alone in the universe'?" she added.
US President Donald Trump dialled in to the space agency's news conference to congratulate the scientists working on the project.
"You're the hottest in space, and we have the hottest country anywhere in the world. So, let's keep it all going. You're a big part of it," Trump said.
Astronomer Jenifer Millard said the telescope will be four times further from Earth than the Moon is, where a lot of infrared space cameras - made to pick up what she describes as "heat light"- operate.
She told the BBC this is to make sure infrared light from the Moon and Earth don't interfere with the cameras.
Nasa's James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, also orbits the Sun around one million miles from Earth, but its field of vision is not as expansive. Nasa's Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits at about 300 miles above Earth's surface.
While Roman will look outward into the Universe, Millard said scientists are also anticipating it will find thousands of new worlds in our own galaxy.
The telescope is named after physicist Nancy Grace Roman, who was Nasa's first chief astronomer in the 1960s and its first female executive.
During her career, she was instrumental in getting the Hubble Space Telescope approved by US Congress and later said its most interesting discovery was dark energy.
The new telescope is similarly expected to revolutionise our understanding of the Universe, including through investigating dark energy. It has a five-year primary lifespan with a goal to operate for 10 years.
Nasa says its "crisp, sweeping surveys will help scientists investigate dark energy and dark matter, discover and characterise exoplanets, map billions of galaxies, study black holes, and explore objects from our own solar system to the edge of the observable Universe."
Dark matter, which is invisible, acts as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the Universe's expansion. Together, they are thought to make up about 95% of the Universe.
"One of our main goals at Nasa is answering the question: are we alone in the Universe?" Fox said at a Sunday morning news conference.
"With Roman, we are going to make this giant leap forward... that is going to allow us to look at these distant, distant worlds and start to really resolve the atmosphere around them to let us know: could they be habitable?"
Millard said, through the work of telescopes like Roman, scientists are hoping to create "enormous cosmic maps" of the Universe at various stages.
"They'll be almost like an onion, so you can peel back layer upon layer... and see how the distribution of galaxies changes through cosmic time," she said.
"What we want to do is use this distribution to try and figure out dark matter and dark energy because we know they exist, we see their effects, but what they are is a real mystery."
![](https://bmkltsly13vb.compat.objectstorage.ap-singapore-1.oraclecloud.com/cdn.sg.dailymirror.lk/assets/uploads/advr_abd5f103ed.jpeg)
summary: Nasa has successfully launched the powerful Nancy Grace Roman space telescope from Florida to explore dark energy, black holes, and other cosmic mysteries. Featuring a field of vision 100 times larger than Hubble and James Webb, the telescope is traveling to a vantage point one million miles from Earth. It aims to discover tens of thousands of exoplanets and help answer whether we are alone in the universe.
key_points: The Nancy Grace Roman space telescope launched successfully from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sunday morning.
It features a field of vision 100 times larger than both the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.
The telescope is journeying to an orbiting point one million miles away from Earth.
It aims to discover tens of thousands of exoplanets and investigate dark energy and dark matter.
The mission is named after physicist Nancy Grace Roman, Nasa's first chief astronomer and first female executive.

title: Ice Island Survives Run-In With Joe Island - NASA Science
author: Lauren Dauphin; NASA Earth Observatory
content:
![A satellite view shows the iceberg after it pivoted out of the fjord into Nares Strait, wedged against a small, brown island.](https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/esd/eo/images/iotd/2026/greenland-sheds-its-largest-berg-of-the-season/petermannberg_oli_20260824.jpg?w=1440&h=960&fit=clip&crop=faces%2Cfocalpoint)
![A satellite view shows a large tabular iceberg at the junction of its home fjord and Nares Strait.](https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/esd/eo/images/iotd/2026/greenland-sheds-its-largest-berg-of-the-season/petermannberg_oli_20260823.jpg?w=1440&h=960&fit=clip&crop=faces%2Cfocalpoint)
Summer is prime iceberg season in Greenland’s glacier-fed fjords, and 2026 was no exception. Especially notable was the berg that broke from the Petermann Glacier along Greenland’s northwest coast in August. Roughly the size of St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands, it was the largest calving event by any Arctic glacier since 2020.
Iceberg calving is a routine part of an outlet glacier’s life cycle. Scientists watch the process closely, however, along with numerous other observations of the ice and its environment, for longer-term signs of instability. Petermann is one of Greenland's largest marine-terminating glaciers and acts as a gatekeeper for ice flowing from the ice sheet into the ocean. Its future stability has implications for sea level rise.
The calving event of summer 2026 was spotted on August 4 by Adam Garbo, a doctoral student in glaciology at the University of Ottawa, in imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 mission. Garbo and an international team of colleagues have been using remote sensing to study and track the glacier's ice tongue.
The team reported that the large tabular iceberg, or “ice island,” measured just over 76 square kilometers (29 square miles) at the time it calved—the largest to break from the glacier since the ice island of 2012 (130 square kilometers). The 2012 calving followed earlier major events in 2008 (31 square kilometers) and 2010 (just over 250 square kilometers).
The August 2026 event could have been even bigger. Garbo and colleagues had been expecting a major calving once one of the large rifts they were monitoring finally cut all the way across Petermann’s ice tongue. “What surprised us was that the calving instead followed a different fracture, producing a smaller ice island than we had originally anticipated,” Garbo said. As of late August, two large rifts remained and were expected to eventually produce new ice islands of roughly 94 square kilometers and 84 square kilometers, though the timing remained uncertain.
![A detailed satellite view shows the iceberg wedged against the small, brown island, with sea ice packed densely to its left and more sparsely to its right.](https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/esd/eo/images/iotd/2026/greenland-sheds-its-largest-berg-of-the-season/petermannbergzm_oli_20260824.jpg?w=1440&h=1100&fit=clip&crop=faces%2Cfocalpoint)
Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College has also been tracking the iceberg, using images from NASA-USGS Landsat satellites, as it drifted down Petermann Fjord toward Nares Strait. In the week since it calved, the berg drifted an average of 3 kilometers per day. It continued toward the fjord’s junction with Nares Strait, where it rammed into a small rocky outcrop known as Joe Island (Joe Ø). The brief encounter is visible in images captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on August 23 (top right) and August 24 (top left). A detailed view of the August 24 image is shown above.
Joe Island sits at the mouth of Petermann Fjord, making it one of the first obstacles a departing ice island meets. Collisions with it—like the one that split the 2010 ice island in two—often mark the start of a berg’s breakup. Petermann bergs tend to be thinner and more fragile than those calved by glaciers such as Greenland’s Jakobshavn and Helheim, and thinner still than Antarctica’s behemoths, Pelto noted.
“We were certainly watching closely as it interacted with Joe Island and were impressed that it survived the interaction without further fragmentation,” Garbo said.
The ice island was estimated to be less than 150 meters thick at the time of calving. Wind and surface currents have swept it out of the fjord, and satellite images show it pivoting away from Joe Island and continuing southwest through Nares Strait. As it drifts, it will fracture into smaller pieces as tides, winds, currents, and melting continue to weaken the ice.
Thicker bergs that calve from tidewater glaciers without floating ice-shelf extensions can drag and even become grounded on the seafloor within the fjord, while ice islands, like those from Petermann, might run aground later in their drift. Many ice islands have become "grounded" off the coasts of Coburg and Baffin islands.
Garbo and colleagues noted that ice islands and their fragments have been known to travel considerable distances, posing potential hazards to marine activities and infrastructure while also distributing freshwater through the ocean as they melt.

As the ice island drifted down Petermann Fjord, it collided with a small rocky outcrop called Joe Island but remarkably survived the encounter without fracturing further. Scientists continue to track the ice island as it pivots into Nares Strait and moves southwest, where it will eventually break apart due to environmental forces.
key_points: A massive ice island measuring over 76 square kilometers calved from Greenland's Petermann Glacier in August 2026.
The calving event was the largest by any Arctic glacier since 2020, though scientists originally anticipated an even larger fracture based on monitored rifts.
The ice island drifted down Petermann Fjord and collided with Joe Island, surviving the encounter without fragmenting further.
Driven by winds and currents, the ice island continued into Nares Strait, where melting, tides, and winds are expected to eventually fracture it into smaller pieces.

title: Oxfordshire science facilities protected from funding cuts
author: Victoria Walton
content:
![The cylindrical doughnut-shaped Diamond Light Source at night. A blue beam shoots up from its centre into the sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/ce62/live/31116b70-e73a-11f0-b42f-5fc5f4eab07e.jpg)
The Science and Technology Facilities Council says the Diamond Light Source, at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, remains operational.
- Published
An Oxfordshire science laboratory has said it will continue its research despite a shortfall in funding.
Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) operates from its base at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, and is funded by the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC).
The government has announced funding will be moved away from the STFC over the next four years, leaving a budget gap of Â£162m due to rising running costs.
But a spokesperson for RAL said the facilities at Harwell had been prioritised and "remain operational", with cuts instead being made through "efficiency savings".
![A sign reads "Welcome, Harwell". It is yellow, blue, white and black and positioned on the ground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1670/live/2022ffc0-9fce-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Harwell Science Campus is home to world leading scientific research
It comes as concerns have been raised by MP for Didcot and Wantage, Olly Glover, over the impact of the STFC budget cuts.
In a letter to the secretary of state for business, innovation, science and trade, Glover warned the move would threaten world-leading scientific research and job opportunities for young people.
"Ultimately, our scientific leadership on the world stage, higher education sector and skills pipeline are all currently at risk of being irreparably damaged. Now is the time to prevent that from happening," he said.
But according to the STFC, the RAL projects at Harwell remain operational, including Diamond Light Source, ISIS Neutron and Muon Source and the Central Laser Facility.
An STFC spokesperson said its budget would reduce by 15% over the next four years "through making efficiency savings in how STFC operates the three major facilities on behalf of the UK".
They added that the organisation was making "deliberate choices to prioritise critical research capability".
A government spokesperson said: "We are not cutting the STFC budget: it is remaining flat over the course of the current spending review.
"To ensure we can drive research that delivers real impact for the public, we are funding R&D at record levels, including Â£38.6bn invested in UKRI over the coming years."
summary: An Oxfordshire science laboratory at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus will continue its operations despite a four-year budget shortfall and funding shifts affecting the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC). While local MP Olly Glover raised concerns that the cuts threaten scientific research and jobs, the STFC and a RAL spokesperson stated that major facilities have been prioritised and cuts will be managed through efficiency savings. A government spokesperson added that the STFC budget is remaining flat and that research and development is being funded at record levels.
key_points: The Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus will remain operational despite STFC funding changes.
The STFC faces a budget gap of £162m over four years due to rising running costs and shifting government funding.
Didcot and Wantage MP Olly Glover expressed concern that the budget cuts could damage scientific leadership, higher education, and jobs.
Major facilities including Diamond Light Source, ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, and the Central Laser Facility will be protected through efficiency savings.
A government spokesperson stated the STFC budget is remaining flat and that overall R&D is being funded at record levels.

title: Scientists Filmed an Alien-Looking Fish Moonwalking Across The Seafloor
author: Ivan Farkas
content:
The expansive, abyssal darkness of the deep sea mirrors the mystique and grandeur of outer space.
Hauntingly bioluminescent creatures shine like nebulae, 'marine snow' full of fish feces glitters like space dust, and alien-ish glowing sharks prowl the depths.
And just like spacecraft, telescopes, and rovers, underwater submersibles can transport us to the oceans' coldest, darkest depths, revealing the creatures that live there.
Traditional taxonomic studies often observed sea animals that were captured, killed, or washed ashore, but modern submersibles let us see them as they actually are, in their aquatic abodes, without destroying them.
This can deliver some revelatory observations.
Researchers in China have just filmed a weird shrimp-like fish scuttling sideways along the seafloor like a crab and even 'moonwalking' backward – a movement that has never been observed in any other fish.
This dynamic behavior is enabled by a dizzying array of features that the researchers got a better look at in action.
Scalicus engyceros, a species of armored searobin found in the western Pacific Ocean, was first described in 1872 and was already known for its 'walk'.
The new footage, from the South China Sea, confirms that these fish use their thick, stiffened fin rays to scuttle around like shrimp and even jump in a jerky leap when threatened.
"These walking fish harbor far more novel behavioral and evolutionary adaptations than previously assumed," says Han Tian, a marine scientist at Sun Yat-sen University and the study's first author.
In the journal Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Research, the researchers also report observations of two other species of armored searobins (family Peristediidae) that were sighted between 350 and 500 meters (1,148 and 1,640 feet) using the human-occupied vehicle Shenhaiyongshi (meaning deep-sea warrior) and the remotely operated vehicle Haiqin.
"By observing deep-sea animals alive in their surrounding environment, we can gain insight into the adaptation and evolution of the species," Tian says.
Based on existing taxonomy, the three peristediid fishes share a common ancestor that lived around 60 to 70 million years ago, developing interesting adaptations to handle their extreme environment.
Several hundred meters below the surface, where the searobins were spotted, some 40 atmospheres' worth of water pressure sits upon one's shoulders – yes, fish have shoulders, sort of.
Armored searobins are covered in bony plates, hence the "armored" appellation.
They also have branched barbels on their snouts that look like a garden rake and act like whiskers, allowing them to physically and chemically sense food or obstacles as they stroll along the seafloor.
As the researchers observed, S. engyceros sweeps these rake-like appendages across the seabed as it walks, "occasionally touching sediment bumps or rocks".
Although this may help with 'sniffing' out food and navigating obstacles, it "seems awkward because it appears inconvenient for walking", the researchers note.
To help with that, armored searobins have two pectoral fins that fan out sideways, apparently for balance.
![This Weird Armored Fish 'Moonwalks' Across The Seafloor](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/dive11-armored-sea-robin-1200x675.jpg)
Like other deep-sea creatures, S. engyceros also sports some big peepers – but they may not be so useful. After so long in darkness, their eyesight might be on the way out.
When the researchers approached S. engyceros in their submersibles, the fish didn't seem to hear or see them coming.
Though one of its eyes did look up at the vehicle's light beam before the animal swam away, possibly to avoid small talk.
"This raises the question of whether this species has not resided in this dark habitat long enough for complete degradation of light sensing," the researchers ponder in their paper, "or whether it may still move upward at times, perhaps into the twilight zone."
![Subscribe to ScienceAlert's free fact-checked newsletter](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/05/FOMO-1200x628-_Dont-miss-the-next-breakthrough_-cosmic-colourful-642x336.jpg)
As for the other armored searobins observed, the researchers sighted six Peristedion liorhynchus individuals in an underwater canyon, a different habitat to the seamount where S. engyceros was spotted.
S. engyceros ' dynamic ambulational abilities certainly set it apart from the dozen or so other fish that have evolved skeletal adaptations for walking on land, including the adorable amphibious mudskipper and the otherworldly, eyeless cave angel fish.
The backward-shuffling, side-stepping S. engyceros may be in a league of its own, but then who knows what else is traversing the seafloor in places humans have never come close to sighting.
![This Weird Armored Fish 'Moonwalks' Across The Seafloor](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/swim.gif)
Fortunately, the future promises many more spectacular deep-sea discoveries, made possible by increasingly versatile submersible technologies.
So, whether it's the goosebump-cresting creepiness of underwater 'backrooms' or golden orbs left by tentacled, virgin-birthing 'spaghetti monsters', the oceanographic Bingo card stretches endlessly.
Related: There Are Fungi in The Ocean, And They May Be Way More Important Than We Realized
"Ultimately, this research will reshape scientific perceptions of deep-sea biodiversity and reveal how extreme marine environments drive the emergence of one-of-a-kind biological structures and behaviors unseen in any other aquatic organism on Earth," Tian concludes.
This research was published in Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Research.
summary: Researchers using submersibles in the South China Sea have filmed an armored searobin species, Scalicus engyceros, exhibiting unique movement by scuttling sideways and moonwalking backward across the seafloor. This behavior is enabled by thick, stiffened fin rays, while rake-like snout barbels help the fish sense food and obstacles. Observing these live deep-sea creatures in their natural habitat provides new insights into their evolutionary adaptations and extreme environment behaviors.
key_points: Researchers filmed the armored searobin Scalicus engyceros scuttling sideways and moonwalking backward, a movement never before seen in any other fish.
The fish uses thick, stiffened fin rays to walk and can execute jerky leaps when threatened.
Branched barbels on their snouts act like whiskers to physically and chemically sense food or obstacles as they move along the seafloor.
The observations were conducted by researchers using human-occupied and remotely operated submersibles in the South China Sea at depths between 350 and 500 meters.

title: Scientists could soon settle age-old question of Moon’s origins
author: Sarah Knapton
content:
![The Moon](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500223682_17882016778500_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqT_6uZA1YnDPyAv-y_8iigLE_MFzZV97jjzAiv1jxVQM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![The Moon](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500223682_17882016778500_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqT_6uZA1YnDPyAv-y_8iigLE_MFzZV97jjzAiv1jxVQM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Scientists may soon solve the mystery of whether the Moon was created by Mercury crashing into Earth.
The British-built spacecraft BepiColombo has been travelling towards Mercury for eight years, and this week begins its arrival phase at the planet, before entering orbit in November.
Although Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, scientists believe it formed further out in the solar system, perhaps nearer to Mars. It has a dense core and a thin crust, leading some experts to believe it hit another planet billions of years ago, stripping away most of its lighter surface material, and knocking it into its current spot in the solar system.
The European Space Agency said there was a hypothesis that ancient Mercury may have been the mysterious object that struck Earth 4.5 billion years ago, creating enough debris to form the Moon.
BepiColombo is carrying two probes and is packed with scientific instruments to assess the mineralogical and elemental composition of Mercury’s surface. This could finally answer the question about where, and how, it formed.
Prof Geraint Jones, the lead project scientist for BepiColombo at the European Space Agency (Esa), said: “Somewhere in the distant past, 4.5 billion years ago, when all the planets were forming in the debris surrounding the Sun, it’s thought that Mercury started forming, created a modest-sized planet, and then it was hit by another large planetesimal, which ripped off its outer crust.
“So that means that the overall density of the material that was left behind was much higher, and that’s why it has the high density it has now. For its size, it’s much more dense than you’d expect.
“Learning more about the interior can help us address this question, see how well that theory holds.”
Mercury’s iron core makes up about 65 per cent of its total mass in comparison to Earth’s core which is 32 per cent of its mass, so the missing surface material must have gone somewhere.
Prof Dirk Schulze-Makuch, of the Technical University of Berlin, has suggested that the Moon may be made up of the missing crust of Mercury, which formed after the impact.
Scientists at the University of Arizona have also theorised that Mercury may have suffered glancing blows with both proto-Earth and proto-Venus, before settling into its current form. It would mean that some of Mercury’s missing surface is now on Earth and Venus.
Another clue that Mercury formed further away from the Sun was found by Nasa’s Messenger spacecraft which orbited the planet in 2011 and 2015.
The mission found that potassium and thorium levels on Mercury were similar to how they appeared on Mars.
![Planet Mercury](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500223707_17882016916060_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqzHDhaW2A9CiilXP0xXZ5zmreqapuikfNyCYuptSHoIo.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“Potassium evaporates very quickly in a hot environment while thorium survives even in very high temperatures,” says Johannes Benkhoff, a BepiColombo project scientist.
“Planets that formed closer to the Sun therefore usually have more thorium as compared to potassium. But on Mercury we see much more potassium than we would expect.
“One theory is that this big impact in the past, in addition to possibly pushing Mercury to where it is today, also stripped away most of the crust material and left behind the dense core with only a thin outer layer.”
BepiColombo is made up of two orbiters – Esa’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and the Japanese space agency Jaxa’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO). The MPO was built by Airbus in Stevenage, Hertfordshire.
The mission will get closer to the planet than earlier spacecraft, allowing scientists to map Mercury’s surface with higher resolution. The team are also hoping to find out whether the planet holds water, and discover whether it is still geologically active.
‘New chapter in our understanding of the solar system’
Scientists also want to know why the surface of Mercury is so dark and suspect that it may be covered in graphite. They also want to find out what is causing the planet’s magnetic field.
Nasa’s Messenger also found organic matter on the planet, and although scientists do not think life will be present, it could help them understand how it began on Earth.
BepiColombo is named after the late Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo, an Italian scientist and engineer from the University of Padua who played a leading role in Nasa’s Mariner 10 mission to Mercury.
Santa Martinez, the BepiColombo mission manager, said: “Mercury is a challenging destination, it’s very difficult to reach, it’s very difficult to operate in because it’s so close to the Sun.
“But what makes this mission really unique is that for the first time in space exploration, we are bringing two spacecraft to the vicinity of the planet, and we are going to put them in orbit around this mysterious body, and this is going to bring to the humanity and to the scientific community unprecedented views of the Mercury planet.
“It’s going to open a new chapter in our understanding of the solar system.”
summary: The British-built BepiColombo spacecraft is beginning its arrival phase at Mercury to help scientists determine if the planet's missing surface material formed the Moon. Researchers theorize that a massive impact billions of years ago stripped Mercury of its outer crust, leaving behind a dense core and potentially creating the debris needed to form the Moon. By assessing Mercury's surface composition and interior, the mission aims to solve this long-standing planetary mystery.
key_points: The BepiColombo spacecraft is arriving at Mercury after an eight-year journey to study its surface and interior composition.
Scientists hypothesize that an ancient impact stripped Mercury of its crust, and that missing material may have formed the Moon.
Mercury features a disproportionately dense iron core and unexpected levels of volatile elements like potassium, supporting the impact theory.
BepiColombo carries two probes designed to map Mercury at higher resolutions than previous missions.

title: Volcano that erupted with strength of a million atomic bombs discovered in England
author: Anamica Singh
content:
A volcano that erupted with the power of one million atomic bombs around 454 million years ago has been discovered deep under England. Scientists say this supervolcano is buried under the east coast of England, with the centre right beneath The Wash. The volcano spans an area of 64 kilometres and is responsible for a layer of volcanic ash found in many countries. This ash layer is present in Poland, Belarus, and also Sweden and Norway. Can it erupt again?
The discovery was made following a fresh analysis of rock samples gathered 80 years ago from North Creake in Norfolk and Claxby in Lincolnshire. The researchers said that the finding changes human understanding of "England's deep geological past". Prof Jenni Barclay, a volcanologist at the University of Bristol, said, "This work is an important step forward in piecing together the geological history of the UK."
The team took the old specimen during COVID and tried using new technology to study it since they could not get their hands on new samples because of the lockdowns. These included crystals as wide as a human hair that formed in molten magma before the eruption. During their analysis, scientists found that the samples taken from Norfolk and Lincolnshire had come from the same volcano and formed at the same time.
![](https://english.cdn.zeenews.com/static/public/updated_logos/googlePreferred.png)
This eruption was also extremely powerful, and the proof was found in Norway. These samples were exactly the same as the ones collected from Norway and Sweden and analysed by researchers at the University of Oslo. This showed that the material from this volcano spread across a large area, including the present-day Scandinavian countries.
Trending Stories
Can this super volcano erupt again?
The finding causes obvious concerns among the common man. What if it erupts again? Allaying all such fears, scientists have assured that this volcano has gone extinct and will never erupt again. Dr Tim Pharaoh of the British Geological Survey (BGS), said, "Unlike faults, which can be seismically reactivated, a volcano can't." He added, "Once it's gone extinct, that's it. Nobody needs to worry about the supervolcano erupting again."
summary: Scientists have discovered a 454-million-year-old supervolcano buried deep beneath the east coast of England, with its center located under The Wash. Spanning 64 kilometers, the volcano erupted with the power of a million atomic bombs and distributed ash as far away as Poland, Belarus, Norway, and Sweden. The discovery was made using new technology to analyze rock samples originally gathered 80 years ago from Norfolk and Lincolnshire. Experts have assured the public that the supervolcano is extinct and poses no threat of future eruptions.
key_points: A massive 64-kilometer supervolcano has been discovered buried under the east coast of England.
The volcano erupted around 454 million years ago with the force of one million atomic bombs.
Its ash layer has been identified in several countries, including Poland, Belarus, Sweden, and Norway.
The discovery resulted from modern technological analysis of rock samples collected 80 years ago in Norfolk and Lincolnshire.
Scientists confirmed that the volcano is completely extinct and cannot erupt again.

title: Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson took the photograph that proved Einstein right about the universe in 1919. So why does history only remember Arthur Eddington's name?
author: Tom May
content:
![A publicity still from the BBC drama Einstein and Eddington shows David Tennant as Eddington and Andy Serkis as Einstein, standing together in period suits in front of a chalkboard.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/p6sZGKNsnEBfiQzxKL8iwK.jpg) 
Almost every photographer has watched someone else get the credit for a picture they actually took.
Usually it's a minor issue: a mistyped byline, a client who thanks the wrong assistant. But in May 1919, it happened on a scale that reshaped our understanding of the entire universe – and the person who ended up with the glory wasn't the one holding the camera that mattered.
Above you can see a publicity still from the 2008 BBC film, Einstein and Eddington, with David Tennant (Dr Who, God Omens) playing English astrophysicist and mathematician Sir Arthur Eddington and Andy Serkis (The Lord of the Rings, Star Wars) playing Albert Einstein.
It's a fair summary of how the story has been told over the last hundred years: two great men, staring down the camera in front of a blackboard, working the problem out together.
And yet the photograph that settled the argument wasn't actually taken by either of them.
A tale of two expeditions
Eddington travelled to the island of Príncipe, off the west coast of Africa, to photograph the total solar eclipse of May 29 1919 and measure whether starlight bent as it passed the Sun, as Einstein's general theory of relativity predicted.
He sat out a tropical storm that didn't clear until an hour before totality, then changed 16 photographic plates blind through drifting cloud, unable to see whether he was capturing anything usable at all.
The best camera deals, reviews, product advice, and unmissable photography news, direct to your inbox!
Only a pair of his plates turned out good enough to measure, and even those gave a fairly loose result: a deflection of about 1.61 arcseconds, with an error margin wide enough that on its own, it wouldn't have persuaded sceptics.
Thankfully for science, a decisive image came from the other side of the Atlantic. Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson of the Royal Greenwich Observatory had travelled to Sobral in Brazil to photograph the same eclipse, as insurance against exactly the kind of weather Eddington ran into.
Their trip didn't go particularly well, either. Their main telescope was ruined by heat that warped its mirror mid-shoot and blurred every star image into a smear.
It was their spare, a smaller 4-inch instrument brought along purely as a backup, that produced the sharpest plates of the entire project: a deflection of 1.98 arcseconds, with an error margin roughly a quarter the size of Eddington's.
That was the shot that actually proved Einstein's theory right. The whole project, though, came to be known as 'The Eddington experiment'.
Technically, that wasn't actually incorrect.
Eddington and the astronomer Frank Dyson – the primary architect of the venture – designed the test and organized both expeditions. Eddington was the one who stood up at the Royal Society in November 1919, told the room that the numbers backed Einstein, and then wrote the popular accounts.
 ![A positive print of the 1919 eclipse plate shows the Moon's black silhouette ringed by the Sun's bright corona flaring against a dark sky.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/8BoZztFSp53AXkjTQaRnmU.jpg) 
 ![A negative image of the 1919 eclipse plate shows the Sun's disc as a bright white circle surrounded by a dark, radiating corona against a pale background.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ubK5v7QLFNV56Dd7PqvAyU.jpg) 
He had the better personal story, too: a Quaker who'd risked prosecution as a conscientious objector during the First World War, and spent those years teaching himself a German physicist's theory that almost nobody in Britain would read.
Crommelin and Davidson, by comparison, were Greenwich Observatory staff doing a job – and they don't appear as characters in the BBC drama at all.
Admittedly that made the script easier for viewers to follow, but it does seem a little unfair all the same. And it especially stings for any working photographer who's seen the same pattern on collaborative shoots.
Often, the name that ends up on the results is the one attached to the idea and the presentation – not necessarily the one who pressed the shutter on the shots that are used.
Eddington obviously deserves credit for designing this groundbreaking experiment and for having the nerve to run it at all.
But the photograph that proved Einstein right came out of a spare telescope in Brazil, operated by two men whose names many people reading this article will never have heard of. Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson: let's remember them now.
Einstein and Eddington is streaming now on Max (formely HBO Max) and Amazon Prime in the US, and has been released worldwide by BBC DVD.
![Tom May](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/9gGAGRPzJeEG2f5kxRw4SM.jpg)
Tom May is a freelance writer and editor specializing in art, photography, design and travel. He has been editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine. He has also worked for a wide range of mainstream titles including The Sun, Radio Times, NME, T3, Heat, Company and Bella.
