summary: This article explores exotic theoretical proposals for interstellar travel, focusing on concepts like warp drives and wormholes. It highlights Proxima b as a prime target for early exploration due to its proximity and potential habitability. The text details the history and physics of the Alcubierre warp drive, including modern theoretical adjustments that could drastically reduce its energy requirements using exotic matter.
key_points: Proxima b orbits the red dwarf star Proxima Centauri at a distance of 4.25 light-years, making it a primary candidate for early interstellar missions.

Proposed in 1994 by Miguel Alcubierre, the warp drive concept relies on contracting spacetime in front of a spacecraft and expanding it behind to travel faster than light locally without violating relativity.

Early calculations showed warp drives required impossibly vast amounts of negative mass, but recent theoretical adjustments by researchers like Harold White suggest the energy requirements could be significantly lowered.

Wormholes, or Einstein-Rosen bridges, are theoretical tunnels connecting different points in spacetime derived from General Relativity, though they remain unstable and require exotic matter to remain open.

title: 15,000 years of solar wind in four hours? A Seattle company gives it a go.
author: Eric Berger
content:
As part of its nuclear fusion processes, the Sun produces a particularly interesting isotope of helium, known as helium-3. Some of this helium-3 escapes the Sun’s gravitational pull as part of the solar wind, a stream of charged particles that emanates out across the Solar System.
Over billions of years, this wind has bombarded every body in the vicinity of the Sun, including Earth’s Moon. Lacking a magnetic field or atmosphere, the Moon’s surface has no barrier to prevent the constant flow of this wind.
This means that helium-3 has been striking the lunar soil, or regolith, for a long time. These helium ions penetrate only a little way into the individual grains of this soil, but periodically meteorites have struck the lunar surface to churn the soil, mixing some of this helium-3 a little below the surface.
The concentrations of helium-3 are not super high, perhaps only 10 to 20 parts per billion in some titanium rich soils, which retain the helium ions better. But they are far higher on the Moon than on Earth, which is largely shielded from the solar wind.
Can the helium-3 actually be mined?
The presence of helium-3 on the Moon has long been an object of fascination for some scientists and engineers on Earth, most notably geologist and Apollo 17 astronaut Harrison “Jack” Schmitt. Long-term, they believe helium-3 could provide energy through a fusion reaction. But in the near term there are more practical uses, such as cooling materials to ultra-low temperatures, medical research, and neutron detection. This makes helium-3 one of the only known materials on the Moon that could plausibly be mined there and returned to Earth for a profit.
For this reason, a handful of companies, including a Seattle-based firm called Interlune, have been interested in potentially mining the helium-3 on the Moon. But before any company can send a full-scale extractor to the Moon to attempt to sift through regolith and collect helium-3, someone should probably attempt to determine whether this is physically practical.
summary: The Sun produces helium-3, which travels via solar wind and accumulates in the Moon's soil because the Moon lacks an atmosphere or magnetic field. Although concentrations are low, helium-3 is valuable for potential fusion energy, cooling materials, medical research, and neutron detection. This has led companies like Seattle-based Interlune to explore the physical practicality of mining lunar helium-3.
key_points: Helium-3 from solar wind has accumulated in the Moon's soil over billions of years.
The Moon has much higher concentrations of helium-3 than Earth due to its lack of a magnetic field and atmosphere.
Helium-3 has potential near-term uses in ultra-low temperature cooling, medical research, and neutron detection, as well as long-term fusion energy potential.
A Seattle-based company named Interlune is investigating whether mining lunar helium-3 is physically practical.

title: What it is like on a 10-hour shift as a paramedic during the summer
author: Liz Beacon; Dawn Limbu
content:
![Paramedics Lee and Sophie smile at the camera as they stand inside the back of the ambulance.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/e648/live/b46ba3e0-a207-11f1-ac57-b5f31f9074ef.jpg)
Paramedics Lee and Sophie responded to four calls during the 10-hour shift where they were joined by the BBC
- Published
The challenges the NHS faces in winter are well known, but sustained hot weather has seen health services face increasing pressure over the summer months.
South Western Ambulance Service Trust (Swast) typically responds to about 3,200 incidents a day at this time of year, but on one day in June - its busiest day ever - it responded to 4,350 incidents.
It received more than 5,200 calls to its 999 control room that day, when temperatures reached a then-record-breaking June high of 36.7C.
Common conditions associated with prolonged periods of hot weather include falls, breathing difficulties, unconsciousness and fainting.
So, what is it like to be on the frontline? BBC Points West reporter Liz Beacon spent a shift with two paramedics in Somerset to find out.
More from the West
During a 10-hour shift on 18 August, paramedics Sophie and Lee responded to four incidents.
One was a false alarm, another saw them waiting until their patient had finished their lunch before heading to hospital, and one involved taking a man with severe stomach pains to hospital. He had not seen his GP and feared he had cancer.
They also assessed a woman experiencing heart palpitations, but could find nothing wrong with her. They were the second crew called out to this patient in 12 hours.
Both Lee and Sophie said they really enjoyed the job, but said it could be frustrating and tiring when they attend calls that turn out to not be emergencies.
![Paramedic Sophie sits in the driver's seat of the ambulance. She has one arm on the steering wheel and the other hand is touching a screen.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/967e/live/83bb4cd0-a128-11f1-8c37-3f30331ac537.jpg)
Sophie says false alarms can be quite common
At one point, the pair were on their way to Minehead Community Hospital to assess an 89-year-old woman who was experiencing heavy, laboured breathing.
But before they got there, they were diverted to a care home resident who had hurt her knee in a fall.
After arriving, paramedics had to wait for the woman to finish her lunch before taking her to Musgrove Park Hospital in Taunton. The care home said it called 999 because the woman could not stand up and her knee was swelling.
Once an ambulance crew is assigned to a job, it has to see it through - even if more urgent calls are being made.
"The radio was going off and there were several general broadcasts for category one emergencies in the area," said Lee.
Examples of category one emergencies include a cardiac arrest, someone who has stopped breathing, or a person who has suffered catastrophic trauma or bleeding.
"We have to switch off to the noise in the background and deal with what we're doing at the time," Lee said.
"It can get frustrating if you start to overthink it when you're on duty."
Another of the day's calls involved a man in Minehead who had activated his personal alarm and was no longer responding.
The team drove to him with their blue lights on, only to discover the alarm had been activated in a test and the man did not need help.
"He could have really needed help," said Lee. "We never quite know.
"So unfortunately, we have to respond the same way."
![Two ambulances parked outside of a hospital.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/01c1/live/6bdcc3f0-a128-11f1-8c37-3f30331ac537.jpg)
Swast operates across the largest geographic ambulance region in England
Adrian South, paramedic and deputy director of clinical care at Swast, said there was "no such thing as an inappropriate call".
"If the patient ends up getting the wrong response, that's an inappropriate response to that call," he added.
South said attending four calls in a 10-hour period was typical for most paramedics, depending on the area they are in.
He added while the incidents the BBC witnessed may not appear like obvious emergencies to some, they highlight a recent shift in the role of emergency care.
"The number of life-threatening emergencies has reduced due to public health campaigns and the work of GPs," South said.
"So now our role is more all-encompassing around the whole end of the urgent health spectrum."
Swast covers the largest geographic area of any ambulance service in England, serving more than five million people.
Between 1 April and 23 August, it responded to 466,165 incidents - an increase of 7.8% on the same period in 2025.
It added that 41.7% of patients it treated from April to August this year were taken to an emergency department.
"If you go back 20 years, every single patient went to hospital, whereas now half of patients don't," South said.
"All of those factors come together in reducing the number of what people would typically think of as a life-and-death emergency situation."

She has a face mask under her chin and her hair is tied into a ponytail.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/0502/live/ef8d63a0-7a02-11f1-bee8-53ce494e1abc.jpg)

She has a face mask under her chin and her hair is tied into a ponytail.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/0502/live/ef8d63a0-7a02-11f1-bee8-53ce494e1abc.jpg)
summary: A BBC reporter joined paramedics Lee and Sophie for a 10-hour shift in Somerset to experience the frontline pressures faced by the South Western Ambulance Service Trust during summer. During their shift, the crew responded to four different incidents, including false alarms and non-urgent cases, while handling background radio chatter about higher-priority emergencies. Officials note that while hot weather brings increased pressure and common conditions like falls and fainting, the overall role of paramedics has shifted to cover a broader urgent health spectrum as life-threatening emergencies decline.
key_points: Paramedics Lee and Sophie responded to four incidents during their 10-hour shift on 18 August.

Their calls included a false alarm from a personal alarm test, a care home patient waiting to finish lunch before going to hospital, a man with severe stomach pains, and a woman with heart palpitations.
South Western Ambulance Service Trust typically responds to about 3,200 incidents a day in summer, but experienced a record 4,350 incidents on a single day in June.
Common conditions during prolonged hot weather include falls, breathing difficulties, unconsciousness, and fainting.
Officials state that the number of life-threatening emergencies has reduced over the years, shifting the role of emergency care to cover the wider urgent health spectrum.

title: Nasa space telescope set to launch after surviving Trump budget cuts
author: Richard Luscombe
content:
A $4.3bn space telescope that Donald Trump tried to kill is set to lift off from Florida early on Sunday as Nasa embarks on the next stage of its quest to unlock the secrets of the universe.
The Nancy Grace Roman space telescope survived two rounds of proposed White House budget cuts, and will embark on a million-mile journey into deep space from a launchpad at the Kennedy Space Center at 7.26am ET, barring late technical issues or intervention from Florida’s notoriously capricious summer weather.
Searching chiefly for exoplanets and clues about planetary formation, it is set to join the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes in the annals of Nasa’s storied history of space exploration.
But as next-generation equipment almost 10 years in the making, the Roman telescope, named for the space agency’s first chief of astronomy, who died in 2018, is many times more powerful than Hubble and will work to enhance the output of its stablemates, both of which continue to operate.
![a black and white image of a woman](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/850e69fcedd6abcbacc50661a0d5745b632c6395/0_0_3000_1688/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
According to Nasa, its 300-megapixel infrared camera will give Roman the same sharpness and resolution as Hubble, but with a field of view at least 100 times larger. The agency says each image will capture a patch of sky about 1.5 times bigger than the apparent size of a full moon.
Roman also contains a specialized instrument known as a coronagraph that blocks glare from stars and makes it easier to photograph planets around them in detail.
Nasa said it expected the images would reveal “giant worlds that are older, colder, and in closer orbits than the hot, young super-Jupiters direct imaging has mainly revealed so far”.
Roman’s destination is Lagrange point 2, a “parking spot” in space about one million miles from Earth, where it will operate in the same complex sun-Earth orbit as Webb, though the two telescopes will remain far apart.
It is not entirely a successor to Hubble and Webb, which were launched in 1990 and 2021, respectively, but was designed to support and advance their missions, while making discoveries of its own.
![Technicians observe the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s solar panels in a cleanroom](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4a37b096f6617fd04687225509bf9d3540165ad5/0_0_6150_4100/master/6150.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Nasa said Roman’s large panoramas would “uncover interesting targets that Hubble could follow up on using infrared, visible, and ultraviolet light to offer a more comprehensive view”, while Webb “can then use its larger mirror and more powerful vision to deliver even more detailed, ultra-sharp observations”.
Roman, meanwhile, can view regions around objects Hubble or Webb observe “to offer context”. Its imagery, which Nasa expects will first come in early 2027 after months of calibration and tests in the telescope’s final orbit, will be made immediately public, allowing the agency, professional researchers and amateur astronomers an unprecedented opportunity for analysis.
“From objects in our outer solar system and exploding stars, to growing black holes and galaxies by the billions, very little will be beyond Roman’s reach,” Nasa said in an online explanation of the telescope’s initial five-year mission, which could be extended to 10.
“Roman will pair a large field of view with crisp infrared vision to scan vast, deep swaths of sky. This flagship mission is designed to help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy, and planets outside our solar system.”
Julie McEnery, Nasa’s senior project scientist for the Roman mission, said the need for it was conceived at the end of the last century, although it was only in 2016 that Nasa began the development stage, and 2020 before it finally approved the entire project and commenced construction.
“One of the motivations for Roman was the discovery that our universe is not just expanding, but that expansion is accelerating,” she said in an interview on Thursday with Sophia Roberts, an astrophysics video producer at Nasa’s Goddard space flight center in Maryland.
“It’s like if you were to throw a ball in the air, and instead of the ball coming back down, it just keeps shooting away. There’s something really fundamental that we don’t understand about the nature of our universe itself, and Roman is purpose-built to address and provide the data that we need to address these questions.”
If the US president had his way, Roman would never have made it to the launchpad. A 2025 White House proposal for what analysts said would be “extinction level cuts” to Nasa’s science budget, including the axing of the Roman project, was roundly rejected in January by Congress, which restored the agency’s 2026 funding level to $24.4bn.
Seemingly undeterred, the Trump administration is trying again for the 2027 fiscal year, seeking a 23% reduction in Nasa’s overall budget to $18.8bn, and a 46% chop for science projects that the Planetary Society said would lead to the termination of more than 50 missions.
Sunday’s scheduled launch of Roman marks the final flight of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket, which Elon Musk’s company is phasing out along with its smaller Falcon 9 rockets to concentrate on Starship, its versatile new workhorse that is planned to eventually carry humans to Mars.
summary: The $4.3bn Nancy Grace Roman space telescope is scheduled to launch from Florida's Kennedy Space Center, having survived multiple proposed White House budget cuts under Donald Trump. Named after Nasa's first chief of astronomy, the powerful new telescope will journey one million miles into deep space to study exoplanets, dark matter, and dark energy. It is designed to work alongside the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes to enhance humanity's understanding of the universe.
key_points: The Nancy Grace Roman space telescope survived two rounds of proposed White House budget cuts before its scheduled Sunday launch.
The $4.3bn telescope features a 300-megapixel infrared camera that gives it a field of view at least 100 times larger than Hubble.
Roman will travel to Lagrange point 2, a location about one million miles from Earth, to support and advance the missions of Hubble and Webb.
The telescope's primary goals include searching for exoplanets and helping astronomers explore dark matter and dark energy.

title: ‘Jellyfish’ on Mars: Image from Curiosity rover goes viral
author: Paul Scott Anderson
content:
‘Jellyfish’ on Mars: Image from Curiosity rover goes viral
![Jellyfish on Mars: Fuzzy black and white view of a rocky hill, with a dark blob just above it with wispy legs trailing down.](https://earthsky.org/upl/2026/08/jellyfish-Curiosity-rover-Mars-August-20-2023.png)
- A previously overlooked photo from the Curiosity rover shows an odd “jellyfish” on Mars. Is it a real anomaly or an imaging artifact?
- The “jellyfish” is a small, dark shape that looks like it is sitting on top of a distant rocky hill.
- There are various possible explanations, but some kind of imaging artifact is the most likely.
The ‘jellyfish’ on Mars
The rovers on Mars sometimes see things that look really odd. Typically, it’s weird rocks or other surface features. But sometimes it’s in the sky. Those usually turn out to be pixel artifacts or other glitches in the cameras. And there’s a new case that’s going viral on social media. The image is from the Curiosity rover, in Gale crater, and is actually from August 20, 2023 (sol 3924 for the rover).
But it was largely overlooked until Kari Sivertzen posted it on X on August 12, 2026. The image shows what looks like a “jellyfish” shape in the distance. The “tentacles” look like they are touching the top of a rocky hill. What is it really?
![Fuzzy black and white view of a rocky hill, with a dark jellyfish-like shape on top of it.](https://earthsky.org/upl/2026/08/jellyfish-Curiosity-rover-Mars-wider-view-August-20-2023.png)
Object or imaging artifact?
It looks intriguing, so what is this mysterious “jellyfish”? Notably, images that Curiosity took less than two minutes earlier, looking in the same direction, didn’t show the odd shape.
The original image is a raw, grayscale image, so not the highest resolution. And the shape only covers about 15 pixels, so quite tiny. The image is from Curiosity’s right navigation camera. The same camera then took another image about 78 minutes later and the shape was gone.
Theories about the ‘jellyfish’ on Mars
Since the shape is absent in subsequent images, that shows it is not a permanent feature of the landscape. With that in mind, there are a few theories, as also mentioned by Amit Surti on Medium.
The possibilities include a cosmic ray artifact, an electronic or transmission artifact and what astronomers would call a transient physical phenomenon.
Cosmic ray artifact?
Firstly: could the “jellyfish” be a cosmic ray artifact? Both the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have seen many of these before. As Surti described on Medium:
Curiosity’s cameras operate in a high-radiation environment. High-energy particles known as cosmic rays constantly bombard CCD detectors in space. When a cosmic ray strikes the silicon grid during a calibration step called a bias frame, it deposits a localized charge. The camera’s processing pipeline later subtracts the bias measurement from the actual exposure. That subtraction converts the bright charge from the particle strike into a dark residual imprint.
The physical movement of charge along the detector’s pixel columns, a process called charge diffusion, combined with the specific readout direction, could produce thin downward-pointing extensions from that dark core. That would explain the jellyfish shape. And because the interaction is momentary rather than persistent damage, the artifact would appear in only one exposure.
A similar shape was also seen in a navigational camera image in 2022, sol 3613. It’s a compelling explanation, but we’d need complete engineering logs to confirm it or not.
Astrophysicist explains mysterious Mars “jellyfish”. Video via Astraveo/ YouTube.
Electronic or transmission artifact?
The shape could also be due to an electronic or transmission glitch. From Medium:
A pixel value can change at multiple points between the camera sensor and the final image file on Earth. Within the readout electronics, inside the flight computer’s storage, during onboard compression, throughout the downlink transmission or during ground processing.
Specific failure modes that produce localized dark regions include: temporary pedestal drift in the electronics, single-event upsets in the image buffer from radiation, temperature spikes from nearby rover hardware triggering dark-current surges, packet loss during transmission generating empty dark blocks and minor mismatches in flat-field calibration files leaving regional residuals.
This could produce a similar dark shape that appears in one image, but not the previous one or the next one.
Transient physical phenomena
Finally, what about something physical, but impermanent? It could be a dust particle or even a dust devil. But to confirm this, data from wind sensors or the left navigation camera would be needed … and both are missing in this case.
The lack of corroborating data shows how difficult it can be to observe an “anomaly” on Mars and try to figure out what it is when there is only one low-resolution image available and not much other data. And most likely, we will see more oddities like this in the future.
Interestingly, some UAP – Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena – have been described as jellyfish-like over the years, such as this one from over a U.S. joint operations base in Iraq in 2018. Or this one – the floating brain – from over the Atlantic on January 1, 2020.
Bottom line: What is this odd ‘jellyfish’ on Mars? Possibilities include a cosmic ray artifact, an electronic artifact and what astronomers call a “transient phenomenon.” The image went viral this week!
summary: An overlooked photograph taken by the Curiosity rover in August 2023 recently went viral on social media for capturing an odd, jellyfish-like shape on Mars. The tiny dark shape, which appeared in only a single low-resolution image from the rover's navigation camera, is most likely an imaging artifact rather than a real surface feature. Experts suggest it could be the result of a cosmic ray striking the detector, an electronic or transmission glitch, or a transient physical phenomenon like dust.
key_points: A Curiosity rover image from August 20, 2023, went viral after being posted on social media in August 2026.
The dark, jellyfish-like shape appeared in only one navigation camera image and vanished in subsequent photos taken minutes and hours later.
The most probable explanation is an imaging artifact, such as a cosmic ray strike or an electronic transmission glitch.
Other theoretical possibilities include transient physical phenomena like dust particles or a dust devil, though corroborating data is lacking.

title: Trump tried to scrap NASA's Roman Space Telescope last year. Now it's ready to launch
author: Josh Dinner
content:
![Illustration of of a space telescope in space, with galaxies, stars and diffuse purplish gas in the background](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/EwPu85UVziqJB4gV35kinK.jpg) 
The hours are counting down to the launch of NASA's newest flagship orbital observatory. The spacecraft recently got its last glimpse of terrestrial light before being encapsulated in its rocket's protective payload fairing last week and is imminently bound for liftoff.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is NASA's next-generation research satellite, and it's currently slated to launch on Sunday (Aug. 30). Roman will lift off atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket at 7:27 a.m. EDT (1127 GMT) from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The scope will then head to sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2 (L2), an orbital sweet spot about 930,000 miles (1.5 million km) away that will park the spacecraft on the side of Earth opposite the sun.
Roman's upcoming launch will cap nearly two decades and $4 billion of development and usher in a new wave of astronomical research into dark matter and dark energy, exoplanet discoveries and the ability to capture visible-to-near-infrared images of the universe that are 50 times wider than the field of view on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). But last year, as Roman's assembly and testing neared completion, President Trump's leaked budget proposal for fiscal year 2026 (FY26) stoked fears that the entire mission could be canceled.
In April 2025, reporting about initial "passback" budget documents outlined a proposal for the largest cut in NASA's history — a 24% overall reduction in funding, with a 50% loss to science programs. The document detailed continued support for missions like Hubble and JWST but allocated "no funding … for other telescopes." The news shocked scientists and engineers across NASA missions, who were suddenly dealt a dose of uncertainty as their job security teetered in political limbo.
For Roman's team, the prospect of abandoning the telescope just before the finish line hit hard. Lisa, an engineer who worked on Roman's team at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland and wished to be identified by an alias, was left confounded at the time. "We're 95% there. If it gets canceled, it would be really ridiculous, and I don't know how I would handle it," she told Space.com in an interview. "This is basically my life's work."
Others working on Roman took the news in stride. Jamie Dunn has worked at Goddard since 1991. He served as Roman's project manager from 2018 until he was appointed director of the center this past June. During a question-and-answer session with a committee of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine on Aug. 10 — part of a congressionally mandated assessment prompted in part by reporting from Space.com about accelerated facility closures and consolidations at Goddard last year — Dunn described a calmer reaction to Roman's potential cancellation.
"Out of the eight years I [worked on Roman]," he told the committee, "we were zeroed out in the president's budget … in at least half of them. Not to be casual about it, but that happens."
When the president's official "skinny budget" proposal was published a few weeks after the April leak last year, Roman's prospects shifted from dire to just worrisome. Instead of cancelling the mission outright, the administration's budget request allocated just $156.6 million to Roman's continued development in FY26 — less than half of what the project received in FY25.
 ![technicians in clean suits in a hangar next to a large rectangular spacecraft wrapped in metallic foil](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/aoHABT2USmdHLUoiQkKLHg.jpg) 
Goddard personnel began working around the clock at a time when government agencies, including NASA, were initiating reductions in force and encouraging civil servants to accept a "deferred resignation" option. Of three skilled technicians working in one department of Roman's team, two left, according to Lisa, which put further strain on the telescope's ongoing qualification testing at the time.
"We're pushing forward to get as far as we can while we have our current funding, and we'll see what happens," Lisa told Space.com last summer. "That amount of funding obviously will make it impossible, in my opinion, to keep schedule, because we can't keep running two shifts with half the people."
On the management side, Dunn tried to keep his team from getting distracted by politics. "Sometimes you've just got to keep coloring," he told the National Academies committee. "We kept working, and I [told the Roman team that] the best thing we can do is deliver on our commitments. And if delivering on our commitments isn't good enough, then what else can we do?"
Lisa said that Roman's mission leadership mitigated the team's panic. "[They] actually did a really good job of telling us, 'We're just going to proceed as we were before … Just focus on the work,' and, 'The best way to make sure we don't get cut is to continue delivering and continue to stay on schedule,'" she said.
Many of the engineers and technicians working on Roman "just put on blinders, put our heads down and kept working," Lisa said. "People were giving up their weekends, and at the same time, there was this compartmentalized knowledge that it could all get cut."
Rather than merely stay on schedule, though, the Roman mission team was pushed to accelerate it. Congress ultimately rejected the steep cuts to NASA in the president's budget request and restored the agency's funding to the previous year's levels. Not wanting to go through a repeat of uncertainty for FY27, Roman mission management began eyeing faster routes to the launch pad.
"They just kept pulling it earlier and earlier, because I think they were pushing to get it off the ground and in space before it could get cut," Lisa said. Eventually, Roman's target launch date moved up to September, and then to the end of August "so that it could happen within this fiscal year."
"In order to stay on schedule at the time, the Roman teams were running two shifts every day and working every Saturday, sometimes on Sundays," Lisa said. The strain took a toll on morale, but their hard work paid off. NASA announced the Roman Space Telescope's completion in April, eight months ahead of schedule, and under budget.
"Lo and behold, it turns out delivering on your commitments means something," Dunn said.
Now, all eyes are turning to watch Roman leave Earth. Having passed all its political hurdles leading up to launch day, Roman has one more major milestone: Launching to space to begin its mission.
Rocket rides to orbit aren't known for being particularly smooth, and after so much time spent worrying about budgets and schedules, Lisa said the part that makes her and her colleagues most nervous now is that it's out of their hands. "The launch vehicle … that's what we kind of don't have control over," Lisa said. "I'm really nervous, because it's just so many people's effort and years of work and sacrifice."
It'll take the telescope 30 days to reach its L2 destination, and there are a few benchmarks it has to meet along the way. Roman will have to perform a few trajectory adjustments, including the mid-course "correction 1" maneuver about 24 hours after launch, which Lisa described as one of Roman's most consequential in reaching its designated orbit.
After nearly two decades of development — and a final year spent wondering whether the telescope would make it to the launch pad at all — the team's focus has finally shifted to Roman's actual in-space operation as it awaits delivery to its new home in the final frontier.

summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is scheduled to launch on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Florida after nearly two decades of development costing $4 billion. The mission faced significant uncertainty last year when proposed federal budget cuts threatened to cancel the telescope just before completion. Despite staffing strains and political challenges, the team accelerated their schedule to finish the project early, and Congress ultimately restored NASA's funding.
key_points: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is slated to launch on Sunday, Aug. 30, from NASA's Kennedy Space Center.
President Trump's leaked budget proposal for fiscal year 2026 previously proposed deep cuts that threatened to cancel the mission.
Congress ultimately rejected the steep proposed cuts and restored NASA's funding to previous levels.
Driven by the budget uncertainty, the mission team accelerated their work to complete the telescope eight months ahead of schedule and under budget.
The spacecraft will travel to sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2 (L2), located approximately 930,000 miles away, to study dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets.

title: Why space weather matters on Earth, and the team trying to protect us
author: Sabrina Lee; Gareth Bryer
content:
![Richard wears a dark blue shirt which is unbuttoned at the collar. He is looking towards the camera with several screens showing images of the sun behind him](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/cc7b/live/942f5120-a09b-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.jpg)
Richard Stone's forecasting team operates 24/7, every day of the year
- Published
At the Met Office headquarters, the screens in one corner of the control centre are focussed on close up imagery of the Sun.
It is here that a space weather prediction team, one of only a small number worldwide, operates 24-hours a day, 365 days a year.
The weather in space has the potential to impact our lives here on Earth in a fundamental way. GPS, power grids and satellites are some of the vital technologies vulnerable to changes in the earth's magnetic field.
As a result, the Met Office has turned to Aberystwyth University researchers to help them improve their space weather forecasting abilities.
![Eight LED screens in an office, with different coloured circles dominating each one. Colours range from yellow to purple. It's not possible to make out the detail of the text underneath](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/4452/live/2ac2ae20-a09c-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.jpg)
Monitoring the activity on the surface of the Sun in the Met Office control room
Space weather is mostly driven by activity on the Sun. Examples include solar flares, which are intense bursts of radiation.
The UK government has included severe space weather in its National Risk Register.
A 2025 estimate by Lloyds, external found that a severe space weather event could cost the world economy 2.4 trillion dollars ($2,400,000,000,000) over a five year period.
The Met Office has been working with key infrastructure operators since 2014 to try to keep us safe from those impacts, by producing forecasts using equipment on earth and satellites out in space.
Richard Stone, from the space forecasting team, said it allowed them "to diagnose anything that's happening on the Sun's surface, provide a forecast and alert the relevant users to be able to take mitigating actions".
![A solar flare on the surface of the Sun](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/97e2/live/18eb8ee0-a2bf-11f1-9024-715001d09aeb.jpg)
A solar flare on the surface of the Sun
Stone said the available technology was incredibly impressive, but still at an early stage.
"We've made great strides since 2014, but observations are still limited," he said.
Despite spotting an event on the Sun's surface around three days before it reaches Earth, there are no more sightings until it reaches satellites about one million miles away.
This gives scientists around one hour to more precisely predict its real effect on Earth and, if needed, warn partners of the mitigation needed to avoid disruption.
"It's like seeing a storm on the east coast of America and then not having any observations until it gets to Ireland," said Stone.
The agency has turned to a group of researchers, led by Aberystwyth University, to improve its forecasting abilities.
The project is being led by Professor Huw Morgan, who is Head of Space Physics at Aberystwyth University, working alongside Northumbria, Durham and Reading universities.
![Professor Huw Morgan is stood in a large lab with a lot of equipment behind him. He is looking at the camera with a wry smile on his face. He has a beard and short hair and is wearing a rusty orange sweater.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/490a/live/26a245e0-a09b-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.jpg)
Professor Huw Morgan, from Aberystwyth University
"This pre-warning is a huge mitigation of the danger posed by space weather," said Morgan.
"For example, it gives the National Grid an opportunity to prepare and avoid power cuts, or airlines can divert their flights from high latitude to safer lower latitudes.
"Compared to forecasting normal weather on Earth, space weather forecasting is really quite a developing field. I mean, it's yet to mature where we can give exact forecasts."
![An image of the curvature of the earth taken from space. The sky is a deep red, with part of the earth in light, while most of it is clearly in darkness, with some flashes of lights to be seen. It's not possible to see where it is, as there's a lot of cloud cover. In the foreground is a part of the space station which looks like a wing.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/7255/live/fef56010-a08e-11f1-84af-1fbec28b23b2.jpg)
The Aurora Borealis, also known as the "northern lights", is perhaps the best known example of space weather
Scientists can already predict which years will be busiest for space weather events, with the Sun following an approximately 11-year activity cycle.
"We'll have some very quiet years, very little space weather, and then it peaks then, at the peak of the cycle then we can have a lot of space weather events, maybe several a day," said Morgan.
The Sun reached the peak of its activity cycle, known as the Solar Maximum, in 2024, which is why more of us saw the Northern Lights - another example of space weather.
But the forecast warnings provided to technology companies and infrastructure operators here on Earth means people have felt very little impact so, despite the Sun's increased activity.
'Wires hummed and crackled'
An 1859 geomagnetic storm known as the Carrington Event is often considered to be the benchmark for a worst-case scenario here on Earth.
Named after English astronomer Richard Carrington, the effects were felt widely, with an aurora seen in the sky across much of the world and disruption to the telegraph network, which had only started operating commercially in the 1840s.
Stone said during the Carrington Event, "even telegraph wires were heard to hum and crackle, and they were able to run the telegraph poles without any electricity because the input was so high".
The concern now is that, without mitigation, a modern day Carrington Event would have significantly greater consequences due to our increasing reliance on technology.
![An official head and shoulders portrait-style photo of Helen Sharman wearing a space suit minus the helmet. She has shoulder length dark hair with a straight fringe. Part of the Union Flag, also known as the Union Jack, is just recognisable in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1408/cpsprodpb/eed0/live/38c55d80-a081-11f1-bfeb-dfb02ea642ef.jpg)
Dr Helen Sharman was selected to be the first British astronaut live on TV in 1989
And the impacts of space weather are not just a consideration for people on Earth.
In 1991, Helen Sharman became the first British person to travel into space on an eight-day mission to the Mir Space Station.
She was taught where to shelter if any space weather were to hit the space station.
Dr Sharman said during the mission she was affected by radiation from outside the solar system, called galactic cosmic rays.
"They come through the materials that spacecraft are made of," said Sharman.
"They come through astronauts' skin, and they're what we notice as astronauts because quite often we see little bright flashes of light on our retinas, as those particles come through the spacecraft, through our skin, through our eyes, and affect our vision in that way.
"The higher up you are as well, of course, the further away from the Earth's magnetic field, the more likely you are to not be protected by the Earth's magnetic field.
"So in low Earth orbit, by and large, we're fairly well protected. This is why, when astronauts go to the Moon, or possibly to Mars in the future, we really need to consider how we can protect them much better from radiation."
More top stories
- ![People seen queuing to get to the top of the mountain](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/4008/live/e1b2fa00-a320-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
  - Published21 hours ago
 ![A young girl with curly hair in two bobbles. She is smiling and looking at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/40cb/live/2c9c4ed0-a20a-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- ![A woman with long blonde hair stands in her garden. Behind her, beyond her garden fence, is a large data centre which looks like a tall warehouse](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/4c7c/live/02b5a460-a2a8-11f1-ab20-f9f4f61e8913.jpg)
summary: Space weather, driven by solar activity such as solar flares, poses significant threats to critical modern infrastructure like power grids, satellites, and GPS. To mitigate these risks, the Met Office operates a 24/7 forecasting team and has partnered with universities like Aberystwyth to improve prediction capabilities. While current forecasting is still developing and provides limited pre-warning time, these efforts help infrastructure operators and airlines take protective measures against potential disruptions.
key_points: Severe space weather is included in the UK National Risk Register and could cost the global economy trillions of dollars.
The Met Office works around the clock using ground equipment and satellites to monitor solar activity and issue forecasts.
Researchers from Aberystwyth, Northumbria, Durham, and Reading universities are helping improve space weather forecasting abilities.
Space weather events can disrupt power grids, satellites, and aviation, but advance warnings allow operators to implement mitigations.
Historical events like the 1859 Carrington Event highlight the potential dangers of severe geomagnetic storms to modern technology.

title: Stunning partial eclipse photographs from across Surrey
author: Danielle Malgwi
content:
![The image shows the crest of a moon against an early morning sky. The roof of a house and a chimney can be seen in the foreground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/645/cpsprodpb/2ef9/live/46c0f640-a2fe-11f1-80b3-bf1a174ac193.jpg)
The eclipse was pictured in Guildford by a Frances B
- Published
The August full moon, also known as the Sturgeon Moon, lit up the sky on Thursday night and was photographed by Surrey Weather Watchers.
The Sun, Earth and Moon also lined up in the night sky to create a lunar eclipse in parts of the world.
The partial eclipse was visible across the South East from 02:23 BST until 06:51. And in many areas, the Moon took on a reddish appearance.
The next lunar eclipse visible in the UK will be in February 2027.
