The next lunar eclipse visible in the UK is scheduled for February 2027.
key_points: The August full moon, or Sturgeon Moon, coincided with a partial lunar eclipse.
The partial eclipse was visible across the South East from 02:23 BST until 06:51 BST.
The Moon took on a reddish appearance in many areas during the event.
The next lunar eclipse visible in the UK will occur in February 2027.

title: How decoding beluga whales’ chitchat may save them – and teach us more about ourselves
author: Emma Bryce
content:
In 2015, the whale researcher Valeria Vergara pitched a small tent at the icy water’s edge on Somerset Island in the remote Canadian high Arctic, shrouded in a freezing fog so thick she struggled to see her own hands. She trailed a cord out to the coast and plopped a hydrophone into the water to record the calls of belugas.
As many as 1,000 of the whales, accompanied by their newborn calves, frequented the surrounding bay. Belugas’ ceaseless chatter, made up of dozens of unique sounds, is crucial to keeping these creatures connected in the dim, turbid waters of the Arctic.
Sheltering back in her tent, Vergara pulled on her headphones at the other end of the hydrophone line and was suddenly immersed in a boisterous chorus of clicks and squeals, whistles, mews and trills. “There I was in my tent, blind, surrounded by fog, with a cacophony of beluga sounds coming to me. And I realised in that moment: they live in a similar kind of visual fog, and yet they are profoundly aware of each other’s presence,” she says.
“It was such an instinctive moment of empathy and understanding: oh my God, this is really what it means to live in a world of sound.”
Ever since the earliest known recording of whale song was made in 1949, researchers have been captivated by the wails, rumbles, clicks, grunts and squeals of their communication.
![A woman outside a tent on a beach looking through a monocular](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4471d86bf3016f6cfcd24ae61b78cadee1333e3c/0_0_5184_3456/master/5184.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Sound is the fabric of these creatures’ highly sociable lives: they sing in breeding grounds, chatter in groups during birth, and echo-locate to help each other find food. Individual species have dozens of distinctive dialects, and the structural makeup of their communication shows parallels with human speech. Whales also produce the loudest sounds of any animal, the same that once resonated through the wooden hulls of whaling ships, unsettling hunters of old.
With the emergence of new analytical technologies, insights into whale communication are amassing swiftly. In an era when most whales are protected from hunting but face myriad other threats, researchers are asking: what clues do their sounds contain to better protect whales from a noisier, warmer and more unpredictable ocean?
The beauty of acoustic data is that it is a relatively easy way to gather information about marine mammals: a single floating hydrophone can record years of sound from passing whales. This eavesdropping has yielded discoveries both delightful and profound.
Beginning with the study of infant whales during her doctorate, Vergara, who is director of the cetacean research programme at Raincoast Conservation Foundation, a Canadian environmental charity, discovered that like humans, baby belugas have to learn to communicate from adults, which involves plenty of charming gibberish along the way.
![The heads of four white whales splashing around together](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/23bcfe6132d2cc369fb31406bda7aa7783f5b3e9/865_126_1690_1353/master/1690.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“It will take them a good two, three years to begin to be proficient at the beluga repertoire. They are clumsy initially. They play with sound – they babble, very much like human toddlers,” Vergara says.
One of the first sounds they perfect is an “acoustic name tag” to identify themselves, she explains. But her more recent work has revealed that the underwater range of these self-identifying calls by baby belugas is 18 times smaller than an adult’s, and therefore easily masked by boat noise. This raises the worry that babies who get separated from their mothers in large beluga pods may become permanently lost.
On the strength of research by Vergara and others, in 2018, Canadian authorities decided to close off key beluga meeting grounds to boats, allowing the “faint, tentative, underdeveloped calls of little calves” to be heard, Vergara says. She sees this as one example of why acoustic monitoring matters, revealing “there are so many things that humans can do”.
![A woman on a small boat with a long lens camera looking at something at sea](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bd13b12298b8703329cf47cf6600cc9736273741/683_0_6827_5464/master/6827.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Belugas are at the chattier end of the whale spectrum, but all cetacean species have diverse vocal repertoires. Some also share distinctive constellations of sound solely within their own populations, teaching and learning from one another. It is a social engine that can drive hundreds of unique dialects within species.
Intriguingly, researchers have found that these dialects often correlate to unique behavioural differences between groups, such as specific foraging and migration habits.
Take the keening whistles, squawks and squeals of a distinct group of 74 endangered orcas that rove around the Canadian part of the Salish Sea. For years, Raincoast scientists have been tuning in on this population’s calls, but with little idea of what they mean. Now, by coupling the recordings with observational drone footage, they are hoping individual calls can be linked to particular orca habits.
The goal is to inform more targeted conservation measures that go beyond “a blanket statement that [shipping] noise is bad, but to say noise interferes with their ability to share food, or [coordinate their hunts] over larger areas,” Vergara says.
It was once a controversial idea that whales have unique behaviours, such as dialects, shared socially within groups, because that is the definition of culture, previously seen as the preserve of humans alone.
Now it is accepted that many species have whole cultural traditions shared between kin – with one of the most enigmatic embodied in the songs of the humpback whale. Only male humpbacks sing, composing units of sound into “phrases”, repeated to form “themes”, a number of which are then arranged to produce unique songs.
“I like to think of this as movements in a symphony, from one to the next,” says Dr Ellen Garland, a researcher at St Andrews University in Scotland, who specialises in songs of humpbacks in the South Pacific.
![A whale seen swimming from 10 or 20 metres away with its eye clearly examining the photographer](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4b3e1537b7fc3b41aeee12ce4942bc70d9cd4207/0_0_7600_5067/master/7600.jpg?width=465&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It is not fully understood why the males sing, whether to attract mates, reinforce male bonds, or gather information about their environments. What is known is that individual groups each have a unique song, and that it is constantly evolving as whales delete and add new themes, which all the males in a population will then learn as one, like a choir singing from the same hymn sheet.
Building on decades of others’ recordings, combined with hundreds of her own, Garland has discovered something extraordinary: an individual song will move in an unstoppable wave between neighbouring humpback populations, spreading from west to east across the entire South Pacific.
“Within a season, [a population will] literally throw what they have out the window and rapidly learn this completely new song from their neighbours,” Garland says. “It’s like abandoning your national anthem for something your neighbour is singing.”
![A sperm whale seen from above](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/01eb8157ccb77c6191252fcc982d3afb619ba3f9/550_0_3502_6641/master/3502.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The animals seem unable to resist novelty, and she is trying to understand why. “No other animal does these rapid and complete population-wide changes, except for humans,” she says. “So we have to draw analogies with human pop music, with human fashion.”
These “cultural waves” are becoming important for conservation. Because whale dialects are associated with other unique behaviour, they can be used to identify whale populations whose habits might make them more vulnerable to environmental threats.
One of the first case studies for incorporating animals’ cultural knowledge into conservation decisions involved sperm whales, says Taylor Hersh, a researcher with Bristol University’s Cetacean Communication and Cognition Group. These animals produce complex clicking sounds, the social glue of their deep-diving matrilineal societies, and the focus of Hersh’s work.
Their sounds are composed of “codas”, each one containing a unique number, arrangement and tempo of clicks. Several codas are common across sperm whale groups or “clans”. But Hersh and the rest of a large international team of researchers discovered that individual clans in the Pacific also have one preferred coda, so effective at distinguishing individual populations that she calls it their “identity coda”.
Why sperm whales use these is still a mystery. “Our best guess is that it reinforces their bond,” she says, adding jokily: “It would be like me – which I would never do – going somewhere and saying ‘American!’ and someone responding with ‘American! American!’ It seems like it’s this way of reaffirming that they’re part of the same group.”
That can function like a geotag, pinging the location of sperm whale clans, and telling researchers whether their behaviours are a good match for local ocean conditions. “In most parts of the world, things are getting worse for animals, and so we need to have the best available information about how to conserve them,” Hersh says.
“Cultural insights, which for sperm whales most easily come from dialects, can be really helpful for doing that.”
Beyond conservation, Hersh likes to be immersed in the sperm whales’ auditory landscape, because it lets her consider the world from the perspective of these animals she admires.
They have “really beautiful societies” structured around female relationships and are peaceful. This leaves a lot for humans to be awed by and learn from, she says. “Anything that knocks human exceptionalism down the peg is good in my book!”
Meanwhile, looking at a population of sperm whales off the Dominican coast, Project Ceti (Cetacean Translation Initiative), a US research nonprofit organisation, is training machine-learning AI on their communication and using it to detect new patterns, with the eventual goal of translation.
This research has revealed that sperm whales use different codas in different contexts, and that with the gaps between clicks removed, some codas produce sounds more like what the researchers describe as “vowels” than clicks.
Dominican sperm whales also change the tempo and frequency of some codas in the presence of shipping noise, intimating that the clicks may carry specific, controlled meanings, according to Gašper Beguš, linguist lead at Project Ceti.
The findings could add up to something profound, he believes. “I think this research is reframing how we think of language,” he says, “and how we can extend it to some species.”
![Two scuba divers in the ocean by a line that holds a large tube with cables running off it](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5f69a9bf26dd5acefa14ca6acb5905d7dcf4ab86/0_0_1024_684/master/1024.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
This is a controversial idea among cetacean researchers, with several saying that similarities between human and whale communication systems is not the same as whales having language in the true sense. But there is broad agreement that understanding more about how whales interact could help us to improve their protection.
The definition of language has long been a legal barrier between those who do and do not have rights, Beguš says. “If you’re showing that there’s a blurry line, that means that we need to push that expansion of rights further to these creatures,” he says, noting that this is not a new idea: Indigenous Polynesian peoples have already recognised whales’ legal personhood.
It is tempting to leap from language to another idea: will we ever speak to whales? Some researchers have attempted experiments where calls are transmitted to whales to simulate a conversational back-and-forth. But these interventions can confuse whales’ cultural exchanges and cause severe distress, meaning playback experiments are now considered ethically fraught.
And Vergara says the question misses the point: “This idea that we are going to talk to whales puts us suddenly at the centre of things. Why do we need to go there for something to be fundamentally important?”
Instead of aiding our understanding, she thinks that “blinds us to discoveries that might be really interesting because of how much they differ from humans”.
Recalling the cacophony of beluga chatter that day in the tent, the question on her mind was not what they would say to us, but how their tapestry of trills and squeals enabled them to survive in their vast underwater world – and what that in turn could reveal about how we can help protect them. “It was such a moment of clarity,” she says.
summary: Researchers are increasingly using acoustic monitoring and new analytical technologies to decode the complex communication systems and dialects of whales. Studies show that baby belugas learn to communicate like human toddlers, while humpback whales share evolving cultural songs across populations. Understanding these acoustic behaviors and cultural traditions is helping scientists design more targeted conservation strategies to protect marine mammals from ocean noise and environmental threats.
key_points: Baby belugas spend two to three years learning their species' communication repertoire, initially babbling like human toddlers before mastering their acoustic name tags.
Canadian authorities closed key beluga meeting grounds to boats in 2018 to protect the faint calls of calves from being masked by shipping noise.
Humpback whale populations rapidly learn new songs from neighboring groups in a process that researchers compare to human cultural waves and pop music.
Sperm whale clans use preferred identity codas and dialects, which help researchers track their locations and inform targeted conservation measures.

title: Where And When To See Tonight’s ‘Blood Moon’ Lunar Eclipse From Every U.S. State
author: Jamie Carter
content:
Topline
Tonight’s deep partial lunar eclipse will be visible across all 50 U.S. states, with skywatchers treated to a dramatic deep partial lunar eclipse. At maximum eclipse, 96.2% of the full Sturgeon Moon will pass through Earth’s dark umbral shadow, causing almost the entire lunar disk to glow a deep reddish-orange at maximum eclipse. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is completely safe to watch with the naked eye and requires no special equipment. All you need is a clear view of the moon and, ideally, a cloud-free sky — and there’s even a chance of northern lights. Here’s when and where to watch the lunar eclipse from across the U.S. — and how to photograph the “blood moon.”
Key Facts
Just as a solar eclipse can only occur during new moon, a lunar eclipse can only occur at full moon. That’s what happens on Thursday when the full Sturgeon Moon will be 100% lit by the sun, so its disk appears fully visible.
While the moon is full, Earth's fuzzy outer shadow — its penumbra— will fall on it, causing it to lose much of its brightness. The full moon will then drift into Earth’s darker, central shadow — its umbra — and a dark lunar eclipse will occur.
It won’t quite become a total lunar eclipse — colloquially called a “Blood Moon” — but the lunar surface is expected to turn a reddish-orange color.
Since Earth’s shadow is much larger than the moon, every lunar eclipse can be seen by a whole hemisphere — the night-side of Earth when the eclipse occurs. This week, that includes the Americas (except Alaska and northwestern Canada), western Europe and western Africa.
Where To Watch From Every U.S. State
Although the entire eclipse lasts 5 hours and 38 minutes, the most dramatic views will come around maximum eclipse, when about 96% of the moon’s disk will be covered by Earth’s dark umbral shadow. Across most of the contiguous U.S., maximum eclipse occurs at:
- 12:12 a.m. EDT on Friday, Aug. 28
- 11:12 p.m. CDT on Thursday, Aug. 27
- 10:12 p.m. MDT on Thursday, Aug. 27
- 9:12 p.m. PDT on Thursday, Aug. 27
- 9:12 p.m. MST in most of Arizona on Thursday, Aug. 27
The partial phase itself begins about 1 hour and 39 minutes before maximum eclipse, at approximately 10:34 p.m. EDT, 9:34 p.m. CDT, 8:34 p.m. MDT and 7:34 p.m. PDT.
Observers across the eastern and central U.S. will be able to see the eclipse from its subtle penumbral beginning through maximum eclipse and beyond, as long as skies are clear. Along parts of the West Coast, the moon rises while the penumbral eclipse is already underway, but before the much more obvious partial phase begins.
What about Alaska and Hawaii?
Alaska and Hawaii are exceptions because the moon will still be below the horizon at the instant of maximum eclipse. In Anchorage, the best visible view comes at about 9:14 p.m. AKDT, shortly after moonrise, while Fairbanks gets its best view at about 9:19 p.m. AKDT. In Honolulu, the moon rises after maximum eclipse, with the best visible view occurring at about 6:50 p.m. HST as the moon emerges from Earth’s shadow. Exact moonrise and eclipse visibility will vary within each state, particularly in Alaska and Hawaii, so check local conditions for your city.
What Will The Moon Look Like?
Although this is technically a partial lunar eclipse, it comes remarkably close to totality. At maximum eclipse, 96.2% of the moon’s disk will lie inside Earth’s umbral shadow, leaving only a thin sliver in direct sunlight. That means much of the moon will appear a muted copper, orange or deep red color — the effect that gives rise to the popular term “Blood Moon.” The exact color depends on the amount of dust and clouds in Earth’s atmosphere, which filter sunlight before it reaches the eclipsed moon. Either way, don’t miss the partial phase leading up to the point of maximum eclipse — you’ll get to see the curved edge of Earth’s giant shadow cross the lunar surface. It’s an awesome sight.
How To Get The Best View
The eclipse is easily visible without binoculars or a telescope, though either can reveal subtle details in the moon’s changing colors. For the best experience:
- Find a location with a clear view of the eastern or southeastern sky.
- Get away from bright city lights if possible.
- Check local cloud forecasts before heading out.
- Use Night Mode or a long-exposure setting on a smartphone to capture the reddish moon.
summary: A deep partial lunar eclipse will be visible across all 50 U.S. states, with approximately 96.2% of the full Sturgeon Moon passing through Earth's umbral shadow. At maximum eclipse, the lunar surface is expected to glow with a reddish-orange color resembling a 'Blood Moon.' The event is completely safe to view with the naked eye, requiring only a clear view of the sky.
key_points: The lunar eclipse will be visible across all 50 U.S. states, though timing and visibility vary by region.
At maximum eclipse, 96.2% of the moon will enter Earth's dark umbral shadow, turning a reddish-orange color.
Lunar eclipses are completely safe to watch with the naked eye and require no special equipment.
Maximum eclipse timings across the contiguous U.S. range from 12:12 a.m. EDT on Friday down to 9:12 p.m. PDT on Thursday.
Alaska and Hawaii are exceptions where the moon is below the horizon at maximum eclipse, offering best views shortly after moonrise.

title: Partial lunar eclipse: All you need to know about watching from Northern Ireland
author: Barra Best
content:
![A red Moon lurking behind a glass skyscraper.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/cf60/live/15d4ce10-8c22-11f0-b391-6936825093bd.jpg)
The Moon could turn red, as it did during this eclipse in Berlin in 2025
- Published
Stargazers have the chance to see a stunning partial lunar eclipse early on Friday morning, as the moon enters Earth's shadow.
At its peak, roughly 93% of the Moon's diameter will be covered, making the event look close to a total eclipse.
For people in Northern Ireland hoping to catch a glimpse, the biggest challenge will be the early start, possible cloud cover, and the Moon's low position in the western sky.
More than 90% of the Moon will be eclipsed shortly after 5am.
![An image showing the phases of the partial lunar eclipse showing first penumbral contact which occurs at 02:23 BST. The main eclipse starts at 03:33 BST. The maximum eclipse at 05:12 BST where 93% will be eclipsed. Moonset is at 06:34 BST](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/1353/live/7ba84540-a135-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
The different phases and times for the partial lunar eclipse in Belfast
What time is the lunar eclipse?
The first phase of the eclipse begins at 02:23 BST when the Moon enters the lighter outer part of Earth's shadow, known as the penumbra.
The much more obvious stage starts at 03:33, as Earth's darker central shadow begins moving across the lunar surface, with maximum eclipse occurring at 05:12, external.
In Belfast, the Moon will be will be low in the western sky at about nine degrees with the eclipse ending at 06:34. In Dublin, it will be slightly higher in the sky and last until 06:38.
Further west, viewers may have slightly longer before the moon disappears. In Enniskillen, moonset is 06:41, external.
This means that visibility will not only depend on cloud cover, but also having an unobstructed view towards the west.
What is a lunar eclipse?
![A diagram showing the Earth positioned in between the Sun and the Moon. The graphic represents how the light travels from the Sun and through a larger portion of the Earth's atmosphere. The shorter wavelength blue light scatters more easily and the longer wavelength red light shines onto the surface of the Moon and reflects back to us here on Earth.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/74e8/live/19f42460-a142-11f1-9311-09d4e1fc9016.png)
The Earth is positioned between the Sun and the Moon during a lunar eclipse
A lunar eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth, and Moon become aligned, allowing the Moon to pass through Earth's shadow.
During a partial eclipse, only part of the Moon enters the darkest section of that shadow, known as the umbra.
The moon is not completely cut off from sunlight, however.
Why could the Moon turn red?
Although Earth's shadow blocks direct sunlight from reaching most of the Moon, some still passes through Earth's atmosphere.
Shorter blue wavelengths scattering more easily, while more of the longer wavelength red light reaches the moon.
"That'll be enough for it to turn a reddish colour," according to Terry Moseley from the Irish Astronomical Association.
"This is sometimes called a blood moon - which is a nice dramatic name - but it's not always the colour of blood.
"It can turn anything from orange to a deep red, but the part near the centre of the eclipse will be the most spectacular."
How to watch the the 2026 partial lunar eclipse
As the moon will be low on the western horizon, viewers will need a clear view towards the west as buildings, hills and trees could block the view as the Moon gets lower toward dawn.
Unlike a solar eclipse, no protective glasses are needed to watch a lunar eclipse - it is safe to look directly at the moon, external.
No equipment such as binoculars or telescopes are necessary, although they could make viewing the changing colours of the Moon's surface easier to see.
Clear sky will be crucial and the current forecast suggests that western areas will more favoured, with cloudier skies for central and eastern parts.
summary: Stargazers in Northern Ireland have the opportunity to view a partial lunar eclipse early on Friday morning, with the peak occurring shortly after 5:00 BST. At maximum eclipse, roughly 93% of the Moon's diameter will be covered by Earth's shadow, potentially turning the Moon a reddish color. Challenges for viewers include an early start, potential cloud cover, and the Moon's low position in the western sky. No protective eyewear or special equipment is needed to safely watch the event.
key_points: The partial lunar eclipse begins with the penumbral contact at 02:23 BST, with the maximum eclipse reaching 93% coverage at 05:12 BST.
Longer red wavelengths of sunlight passing through Earth's atmosphere can cause the Moon to turn a reddish or orange color.
Viewers need an unobstructed view towards the western horizon because the Moon will be positioned low in the sky.
No protective glasses, binoculars, or telescopes are required to safely watch a lunar eclipse.
Visibility will depend on local weather, with western areas currently favored by the forecast while central and eastern parts face cloudier skies.

title: Lab supply companies have been selling antibodies using manipulated images
author: John Timmer
content:
Antibodies play a central role in your body’s immune defense. But they’re also nearly ubiquitous in biological research, being essential for several widely used lab techniques. While some researchers need to go through the process of producing their own antibodies, antibodies to many key proteins are commercially available and can be ordered for overnight delivery.
In May, however, Reese Richardson, a post-doc at Northwestern University, discovered that some of the images used to demonstrate how these antibodies performed in lab experiments had been subject to image manipulation—the sorts of changes that would get a paper retracted if they had appeared in the academic literature. The manipulations ranged from removing background noise to copying and pasting data to fabricate results. Now, he has done a more exhaustive search and found problematic manipulations in images used to market over 17,000 commercial antibodies.
Antibodies are useful in the lab because the immune system generates them to recognize specific proteins. While those proteins typically appear on the surface of pathogens, the immune system doesn’t know where a given protein it encounters comes from. So, if you inject an animal with your protein of interest, it will typically generate antibodies to recognize that.
That recognition can be incredibly useful. If you prepare cultured cells appropriately, for example, you can use these antibodies to tell you where in the cell the protein is located. Similarly, you can use them to find out which tissues in an organ or embryo make your protein. Finally, you can collect all the proteins from a cell, separate them on a gel, and then see where the protein ends up, telling you whether it’s made, if it’s chemically modified, et cetera.
summary: Commercial antibodies are essential tools in biological research, used to locate and analyze specific proteins in lab experiments. A post-doc researcher recently discovered that several lab supply companies have been using manipulated images to market their commercial antibodies. Following an exhaustive search, problematic image manipulations—ranging from noise removal to fabricated results—were found in listings for over 17,000 commercial antibodies.
key_points: Commercial antibodies are widely used in biological research for techniques like tracking proteins in cells and tissues.
A researcher discovered that lab supply companies were using manipulated images to demonstrate antibody performance.
Manipulations found in marketing materials ranged from removing background noise to copying and pasting data to fabricate results.
Problematic image manipulations were identified in images used to market over 17,000 commercial antibodies.

title: The world’s largest camera has taken its most mind-blowing images yet | BBC Science Focus Magazine
author: Lily Watts
content:
Sitting high in the Chilean Andes, the Vera C Rubin Observatory is home to the largest digital camera ever built – a machine designed to capture the Universe in unprecedented detail. Construction began in 2015, and the observatory released its first-ever images in June 2025, marking the start of its ten-year mission.
Its 8.4m (28ft) telescope houses a camera roughly the size of a small car and weighing around three tonnes. It captures 3,200-megapixel images so detailed that a single one would require around 400 Ultra HD TVs to display at full resolution.
So, what will it actually photograph? Every three nights, the observatory will sweep across the entire southern sky, photographing every visible galaxy, star and asteroid. By repeating this survey for a decade, astronomers will create the most detailed time-lapse of the changing Universe ever assembled.
Collecting around 10 terabytes of data every night, the observatory will help scientists map the invisible influence of dark matter, discover previously unseen asteroids, and catch distant stars in the instant they explode as supernovae.
Here's a look back at what it's captured over its first year in operation.
Trifid and Lagoon Nebulae
![A pink nebula sits amongst a star filled orange background.](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/914385ba-20f2-414d-a059-ddd8692389d4/noirlab2521b-1.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
One of the first images taken by the Vera C Rubin Observatory was this photograph of the Trifid and Lagoon Nebulae. It was crafted from 678 exposures, taken over just 7.2 hours, creating about two trillion pixels of data.
The final image is nearly 5 gigapixels and reveals swirling clouds of gas and dust where stars are being born around 4,000 to 5,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius.
The pink and blue clouds of the Trifid Nebula sit above the Lagoon Nebula, showcasing Rubin’s ability to capture enormous swathes of the Milky Way with extraordinary depth and clarity.
Take a tour through the spectacular star fields here.
A star city
![Globular cluster](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/20ad29f9-07d4-461a-94a8-b881cbeec9d7/Triffid-GC-Purp.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
This close-up shot zooms in to reveal the tens of thousands of stars within the globular cluster NGC 6544.
It is one of around 150 such clusters orbiting the Milky Way. The star-filled clusters can be found around most galaxies, and many of the stars within them are almost as old as the Universe itself.
Cosmic treasure chest
![a expansive image showing a variety of different coloured galaxy and stars of varying sizes.](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/93852957-0983-4b12-a008-cd1a58c77d82/noirlab2521a.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
This high-resolution image of the southern region of the Virgo Cluster, located about 55 million light-years away, was another of the first images released to showcase Rubin’s incredible potential.
Almost every dot in this image – other than a handful of bright red and blue stars located in our own Milky Way – is a galaxy. It’s estimated there are around 10 million in this one image, but this is only 0.05 per cent of the 20 billion Rubin will catalogue over the next 10 years.
Rubin will return to this same region many times over the next decade, catching brief but important events, such as supernovae and flares from stars being consumed by black holes.
Close-up of the Virgo Cluster
![A purple spiral galaxy with a smaller one imaged in the top left corner of the image, surrounded by black starry sky.](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/5b09b81f-93fb-490d-bedc-38fb45092702/noirlab2521ak.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
Zooming in on an individual galaxy (seen in the bottom right of the previous image) reveals just how detailed Rubin’s images are.
The dust lanes on the spiral arms are clearly visible, while many of the ‘dots’ surrounding it can now clearly be made out as distant galaxies as well.
Bochum 14
![](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/200d42dc-4c81-4130-b847-5cf6f33b4d48/Bochum-14.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
Bochum 14 is an open cluster, meaning it is a group of stars bound loosely together by gravity.
The cluster is completely invisible to the naked eye, but Rubin is able to reveal its many stars against a colourful background of clouds.
An ocean of stars
![Star field](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/d1241c1d-819e-43d3-9485-a65856c4c3ec/Ocean-of-Stars-Purp.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
This 1.7-gigapixel image shows a field of stars in the constellation of Lupus, and contains millions of stars as well as distant galaxies beyond.
The view is covered with a wispy sheen of galactic cirrus – the clouds of interstellar gas and dust found throughout the Milky Way.
Close-up on the ocean of stars
![](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/c28f7db7-6738-4ae8-b366-98f167f76dab/OceanofStars_cee_CC12-crop4-1-e1783692499372.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
Rubin uses six different filters, each capturing a different wavelength (or colour) of light. Astronomers can use this colour information to learn things about their size, temperature and age.
For instance, blue stars are generally more massive, hotter and younger, while red stars are generally cooler, smaller and older.
Messier 21
![](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/8bc09b16-173f-4c16-a316-20c6234b3b4e/Messier-21-Purp.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
Rubin captures another open cluster, named Messier 21. All the stars within it are around 6.6 million years old, suggesting that they all formed at the same time, perhaps in the same stellar nursery.
The cluster is mainly made up of dim stars, but to Rubin’s sharp eye, they seem to shine brightly.
A colourful spiral
![](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/3df29b01-3643-4c80-91c4-e6cffea04572/OceanofStars_cee_CC12-crop8-1.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
A close-up of a spiral galaxy captured by Rubin. Dark tendrils of dust wrap around the central region, while the outer rim is ringed with blue stars.
Barred spirals
![](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/33445ea8-4eca-49a5-b56e-895269eb5c7f/OceanofStars_cee_CC12-crop6-1.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
Here, Rubin is able to capture enough detail to clearly make out the barred structure of a spiral galaxy.
These are galaxies which have a long, central bar-shaped structure of stars, with spiral arms extending from the ends.
Around two-thirds of spiral galaxies are barred, including the Milky Way, though most aren’t quite as pronounced as this one.
Cosmic broccoli
![](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/4c9d8419-cfe7-435a-a5e4-9959ceff3e95/rubin-romanesco.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
The first-ever images taken by Rubin weren’t of giant galaxies or stars, but of something much more humble – a head of Romanesco, a broccoli-like vegetable.
The team projected the image of the vegetable onto the sensor using a pinhole camera to test whether the optical elements were all working together.
The resulting image, taken in September 2020, was the first 3,200-megapixel digital photograph, making it the largest single image ever taken.
Fitting the camera’s sensor
![A Mechanical Engineer is looking at a circle of sensors for the vera rubin telescope.](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/eff4cbc7-7a88-49b4-9a33-c4f5c609e91e/slac-50212638783_377a3e18a4_o-CC.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
A camera as big as Rubin’s needs an equally big sensor, and Rubin’s is made up of 21 Raft Tower Modules (RTM) – 144 megapixel sensors made of nine separate CCD chips.
Here, mechanical engineer Travis Lange carefully monitors the installation of the 14th RTM. It proved to be one of the most difficult of the bunch, requiring multiple stops and conferences to sort out its installation.
Rubin’s first look at the night sky
![The oval shapped LSST camera in the vera rubin telescope is spinning, captured with a slow shutter, this leaves a trail of yellow and orange lights with the starry night sky seen above it.](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/ee91ea55-a768-4986-a3b9-46b980f21c3b/noirlab2521u.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
Rubin begins its mission to map the sky every night, shortly after darkness falls on Cerro Pachón, Chile. This time-lapse shows it slewing back and forth across the night sky.
Dealing with the data deluge
![a brightly coloured red yellow and green nebula with written data in code down the left hand side and parts of the imaged circled, to visualise the Rubin Science Platform.](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/cec9b34c-ab0b-4c96-859a-71b8a588e9e3/ComingSoon-RubinData.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
Rubin captures a new 8-gigabyte image every 40 seconds. That’s a lot of data to deal with, and so the Rubin team have developed a streamlined system to handle it all.
Take this image of the Rosette Nebula. Within seconds of being taken, the data would have been transferred to a local facility and automatically compared to a reference image.
This would highlight any differences, such as those in yellow circles, and generate an alert. There are around 10 million alerts every night, many of which are imaging artefacts, asteroids or satellites.
Some, however, are much larger cosmic events, such as supernovae. When Rubin spots one of these, the team sends out an alert to the astronomical community. That way, observers around the world can rush to their own telescopes and catch it before it fades away.
3D Animation of asteroids discovered by Vera C Rubin Observatory
One thing Rubin has to contend with is asteroids. They often zip across the field of view, leaving bright streaks in images that have to be removed.
It does mean, however, that the telescope is ideal for discovering these space rocks. By April 2026, the telescope had discovered around 11,000 new asteroids, including 33 near-Earth asteroids.
This animation shows previously known asteroids in dark blue and those discovered by Rubin in light teal.
Vera C Rubin Observatory under the Milky Way
![A low wide-angle shot of the vera rubin telescope with an arching milkyway and star-lit sky going directly over the top of it.](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/975d2a6c-5ea2-4d21-8ec1-ead025205273/41c584a0-5ba5-4e3d-9902-8796879eecda/frame1frame7_blended_fused-CC.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=371edb8f-b239-4903-a361-8ebfed914cc5)
The Vera C Rubin Observatory sits on the remote Cerro Pachón in Chile, far away from urban light pollution. Located 2,647m (8,684ft) above sea level, the air is extremely clear and dry, creating the perfect conditions to image the sky night after night without interruption.
Read more:
summary: Located in the Chilean Andes, the Vera C Rubin Observatory houses the world's largest digital camera to capture unprecedented, high-resolution images of the universe. Over its ten-year mission, the observatory will repeatedly survey the southern sky every three nights to create a detailed time-lapse, collecting massive amounts of data to track galaxies, stars, supernovae, and asteroids. Its initial test image in 2020 famously featured a head of Romanesco broccoli before it began releasing stunning deep-space photographs of nebulae, star clusters, and distant galaxies.
key_points: The Vera C Rubin Observatory features a three-tonne, car-sized digital camera capable of capturing 3,200-megapixel images.
The observatory's ten-year mission involves sweeping the southern sky every three nights to map galaxies, discover new asteroids, and catch supernovae.
The facility handles about 10 terabytes of data nightly, generating millions of alerts for transient cosmic events and anomalies.
The very first 3,200-megapixel image taken by the camera in September 2020 was of a head of Romanesco broccoli used to test its optical elements.

title: World-first test sends information through light beams without loss
author: Mrigakshi Dixit
content:
A laser beam shot across a university campus may have just solved one of telecommunication’s oldest problems.
Researchers at Wits University (South Africa) and the University of Bordeaux (France) have demonstrated a method to transmit optical data through open air without needing complex systems to correct for atmospheric distortion.
Sending data through open air has always been a messy thing. Earth’s atmosphere is chaotic. Swirling pockets of warm and cold air twist, scatter, and scramble light signals, often turning to heavy computing power and expensive adaptive optics just to piece the broken data back together.
Now, a world-first experiment laser shows we can simply ignore the distortion altogether.
The team successfully transmitted data through turbulent open air with its integrity entirely untouched. And it all came down to topology.
“We create and transmit these particle-like topologies of light through a 270-meter free-space optical link, revealing their robustness across a wide variety of conditions and turbulence strengths,” the study noted.
The coffee mug trick
Topology is a branch of mathematics concerned with properties that stay constant even when an object is stretched, twisted, or squished.
“To explain its benefits, we can liken it to how a coffee mug can be reshaped into the form of a doughnut,” said Prof Andrew Forbes, Head of the Structured Light Lab in the Wits School of Physics.
“Despite their very different shapes, both have a single hole. You can stretch or distort them without changing that fundamental property. In the same way, the light beam can become badly distorted while its topological information remains unchanged,” Forbes added.
The team applied this concept to light, encoding information into exotic, particle-like magnetic structures called skyrmions. Encoding information into the light’s topological profile gives the data an invisible layer of armor, rather than relying on its raw brightness or color.
To put the theory to the test, skyrmion-encoded laser beams were fired across hundreds of meters between two buildings on the Wits West Campus in Johannesburg. The light hit real-world heat, wind, and atmospheric noise.
When the light reached the receiver, the shape of the beam was utterly mangled. But surprisingly, the underlying topological data remained completely intact.
As a result, data was transmitted through the open air with over 98 percent fidelity in most conditions, dropping to only 86 percent under extreme turbulence.
Laser’s best possible use in space missions
Fiber-optic cables protect light signals by shielding color, intensity, and polarization from external disturbances. In contrast, sending unguided light through open air leaves these signals far more vulnerable to environmental disruptions like atmospheric turbulence.
Until now, free-space optical (FSO) communication systems required constant, real-time recalculations to undo the damage caused by the atmosphere. Receivers had to measure the distortion and fire off dynamic hardware corrections just to read a clean signal.
But now, with this new approach, the topology survives the chaos. Therefore, the receiver can read the encoded payload directly without needing to clean up the beam first.
And of course, the usage will be huge if scaled. Removing the need for heavy corrective hardware could lower the energy and computing demands for long-distance optical networks.
Particularly, the development could be beneficial in deep-space missions, high-speed satellite downlinks, and quantum cryptography. Closer to home, it might bridge the digital divide without laying miles of costly fiber-optic cable. The tech could soon give rural and isolated communities affordable, high-speed internet beamed straight through the sky.
summary: Researchers from Wits University and the University of Bordeaux have successfully transmitted optical data through turbulent open air without the need for complex distortion-correcting hardware. By applying mathematical topology to encode information into particle-like structures called skyrmions, the team protected the data's integrity against environmental disturbances. The method achieved over 98 percent fidelity in most conditions during tests across a 270-meter campus link. This breakthrough could significantly reduce energy and computing demands for long-distance optical networks, space missions, and rural internet delivery.
key_points: Researchers successfully transmitted data via laser through 270 meters of turbulent open air without using adaptive optics to correct for atmospheric distortion.
The method relies on topology by encoding information into particle-like magnetic structures called skyrmions, keeping the core data intact despite a mangled beam shape.
Data transmission achieved over 98 percent fidelity in most conditions and 86 percent under extreme turbulence.
This technology eliminates the need for heavy corrective hardware, which can lower energy and computing demands.
Potential applications include deep-space missions, high-speed satellite downlinks, quantum cryptography, and providing affordable internet to rural areas.

title: 'You just saved the video dish': Two astronauts complete spacewalk to replace ISS antenna
author: Robert Z Pearlman
content:
![two astronauts in white spacesuits work near a large antenna dish outside a space station with a blue and white planet as their backdrop](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/iVzqA5rWsKrkbNBXgRqKNP.jpg) 
"Houston, we have a working comm link again."
Thanks to the efforts of two astronauts, such a call is possible again using one of two Space-to-Ground antennas outside the International Space Station (ISS). The pair finished the replacement of a faulty dish assembly during a spacewalk on Tuesday (Aug. 25).
Anil Menon of NASA and Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency (ESA), who previously removed a faulty dish during a spacewalk on Aug. 18, installed a spare in its place and moved the broken assembly from a temporary to more permanent storage location along the station's backbone truss.
 ![an astronaut in a white spacesuit with red stripes works alongside a large antenna dish outside of a space station](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SPgTQCYqT3pYMKmyF74r3n.jpg) 
With Menon positioned at the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and Adenot traversing by handrails to join him, the two Expedition 75 crewmates first retrieved a spare Space-to-Ground Antenna (SGANT) from an external stowage position. Menon and the spare dish were then maneuvered to the Z-1 truss, where it was mounted and connected to the station's power and data systems.
Menon and Adenot then retrieved the faulty antenna, which they had stowed on the Z-1 truss during the prior spacewalk. Menon (on the arm) moved it to external stowage platform-3 (ESP-3) on the starboard side of the truss.
The replacement work became necessary after the SGANT ceased being able to track NASA's data and relay satellites, rendering it unusable, beginning last November. A second antenna has been in use since, continuing the transmission of voice and critical data, but this repair re-established redundancy to the system.
"On behalf of CAPCOM and I, we're going to count down like a bolt: '3, 2, 1… You just saved the video dish, you just saved the video dish,'" sang astronaut Anne McClain from Mission Control at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, parodying the The Buggles' 1979 hit "Video Killed the Radio Star."
"Oh my god, it is hard to top that," replied Menon, who could be heard laughing along with Adenot. "I want to thank the entire team on executing this complex, time-critical operation successfully."
Tuesday's spacewalk began at 8:27 a.m. EDT (1227 GMT) and was completed exactly 6.5 hours later, at 2:57 p.m. EDT (1857 GMT).
The extravehicular activity (EVA) was the 283rd in support of ISS assembly, maintenance and upgrades. It was Menon's third EVA, increasing his total spacewalking time to 19 hours and 20 minutes. It was the second time that Adenot worked in the vacuum of space, raising her time on EVA to 12 hours and 53 minutes after becoming the first woman and fifth citizen of France to perform a spacewalk.
This was the sixth outing from the International Space Station this year, the third EVA for Expedition 75 and the 98th spacewalk using U.S. extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits at the station.

Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE.com, a daily news publication and community devoted to space history with a particular focus on how and where space exploration intersects with pop culture. Pearlman is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018.
In 2009, he was inducted into the U.S. Space Camp Hall of Fame in Huntsville, Alabama. In 2021, he was honored by the American Astronautical Society with the Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History. In 2023, the National Space Club Florida Committee recognized Pearlman with the Kolcum News and Communications Award for excellence in telling  the space story along the Space Coast and throughout the world.
summary: Two astronauts successfully completed a 6.5-hour spacewalk to replace a faulty Space-to-Ground antenna outside the International Space Station. NASA's Anil Menon and ESA's Sophie Adenot installed a spare dish assembly and relocated the broken hardware to a permanent storage location. The repair re-established crucial system redundancy after the original antenna stopped functioning last November.
key_points: Astronauts Anil Menon and Sophie Adenot completed the spacewalk on Tuesday, August 25.
The spacewalk lasted exactly 6.5 hours, running from 8:27 a.m. to 2:57 p.m. EDT.
The mission replaced a faulty Space-to-Ground antenna dish that had been unusable since last November, restoring system redundancy.
The astronauts retrieved a spare antenna from external stowage, mounted it to the Z-1 truss, and moved the broken assembly to external stowage platform-3 (ESP-3).

title: Wake up early for Friday’s partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it
author: Ruth Wright
content:
At maximum eclipse on 27–28 August, Earth’s dark umbral shadow will cover 96% of the Moon’s face - an almost total eclipse.
Europeans will be treated to a “very deep” partial lunar eclipse in the early hours of Friday (28 August) morning, just before dawn.
A partial eclipse always happens about two weeks before or after a solar eclipse, so this one follows the total solar eclipse that captivated Europeans earlier this month.
During a partial eclipse, an imperfect alignment of the Sun, Earth and Moon means a Full Moon passes through only part of Earth’s shadow in space. The shadow grows and then recedes without ever entirely covering the Moon, creating a rare celestial phenomenon.
Friday’s is a Full Sturgeon Moon, named after North America’s largest fish. The moon could turn a rusty red as it gets 96.2 per cent covered by Earth’s dark inner shadow. The change of colour is caused by Earth: “the edge of Earth’s shadow in space has a reddish glow that comes from sunlight streaming through the atmosphere that surrounds our planet”, according to timeanddate.
You won’t need the special glasses that were necessary to safely view the total solar eclipse earlier this month. Looking directly at the moon during a partial eclipse is totally safe.
If you happen to have binoculars or a telescope, they will make the shadow clearer to see.
Location and weather will determine where in Europe that will get the best view of the eclipse. The places facing west with the least cloud cover will get the most spectacular experience.
If you won’t be able to see the eclipse in person, it will be streamed during a live show by timeanddate on YouTube.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Spain
Just like with the solar eclipse, Spain will get the best views. The lunar eclipse will be visible from anywhere in the Iberian Peninsula, the Balearic Islands, the Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla, provided the skies remain clear with no clouds.
There will be a difference in viewing time, however. In central and eastern Spain, the Balearic Islands, as well as Melilla, the moon will set before the partial eclipse has finished, whereas in the rest of the country, including the Canaries and Ceuta, you will be able to see the whole process of the eclipse.
The moon will rise in Spain at 9.01pm on 27 August and set at 7.47am on 28 August. The partial phase of the eclipse will begin at 4.34am and end at 7.52am – one hour earlier in the Canary Islands.
The peak of the eclipse, which is when Earth’s shadow covers the largest percentage of the moon, will occur at approximately 6.12am, just before sunrise. At that moment, Earth’s shadow will be projected onto 93 percent of the lunar disk.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Italy
Based on current weather forecasts, some of Italy’s biggest cities are set to have the best views: Naples, Rome and Venice are forecast to have the least cloud cover, meaning they should see a 93 per cent eclipse. Bologna is one of the next best, followed by Turin. Genoa and Milan will also have 93 per cent coverage but they are forecast to be very cloudy.
The partial eclipse will start at 03.23am in Italy, it will be at best coverage at 06.12am and it will end at 09.01am.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in France
Current weather forecasts are predicting a lot of cloud and some rain for Friday morning in France so it may not be the best place for a viewing.
The moon will not begin crossing into Earth’s shadow until around 03.20am, with the colouration effects seen around 04.34am. The peak of the event – when the majority of the moon is in the Earth’s shadow and the red colour its deepest – will take place at around 06.13am. At this point however, the moon will be only around 8° above the horizon, and early morning sunshine may interfere.
Marseille and Strasbourg currently have the best chance at a viewing as they’ll have low cloud cover, though there may be heavy rain or lightning.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Portugal
Anyone in Portugal wanting to catch the partial lunar eclipse from the start will be in for an early start - it begins at 02.23am local time and ends at 08.01am.
Lisbon and Amadora currently have the clearest skies forecast, with Braga and Coimbra also in with a good chance.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Germany
As with the rest of the Central European Summer Time time zone, the eclipse will be at its best at 06.13am in Germany. This is after the Moon has set and the Sun has risen in eastern Germany. It begins at 04.33am.
In the far west of the country, however, the rise and set times for the Sun and Moon are delayed by a little more than half an hour, so that more of the eclipse will be visible. The Moon’s exit from the umbra at 7:53am will, in any case, occur long after sunrise and moonset as seen from Germany, according to the Haus der Astronomie.
Read more
