![Daisy Dobrijevic](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/pkTdGWpESciNKAMSD6DjD4.jpg)
Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.
Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.
She will be a guest speaker aboard HX's Solar Eclipse Expedition in August 2026 and will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.
summary: The sun unleashed a powerful M6.9 solar flare from sunspot region 4513, triggering a moderate radio blackout across Africa, Europe, and the Arctic. The eruption also hurled a coronal mass ejection (CME) into space, which models predict could deliver a glancing blow to Earth. This incoming CME, combined with an expected high-speed solar wind stream, may enhance geomagnetic conditions and boost northern lights activity.
key_points: An M6.9 solar flare erupted from active sunspot region 4513, peaking at 6 a.m. EDT.
The eruption caused a moderate (R2) radio blackout over parts of Africa, Europe, and the Arctic.
NASA models predict a slow-moving coronal mass ejection (CME) could deliver a glancing blow to Earth on Friday, August 28.
A high-speed solar wind stream arriving around August 27 could combine with the CME to enhance geomagnetic and aurora activity.

title: The Transmitter’s reading list for 2026
author: Francisco J Rivera Rosario
content:
![Covers of The Transmitter's summer book picks.](https://www.thetransmitter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NeuroBooksSummer-2026-1200.png)
Five new neuroscience books, and other notable titles from 2026
The Transmitter’s summer reading list includes an autopsy of the Human Brain Project, an overview of the neuroscience of motherhood and a memoir from a pioneer in Huntington’s disease research.
“A Mother’s Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution” by Susana Carmona (MIT Press)
In a 2024 Nature Neuroscience paper, Susana Carmona analyzed brain imaging data from more than 100 pregnant women in Spain, making it one of the most detailed studies of what happens in the human brain during gestation. In her new book “A Mother’s Brain,” she provides a comprehensive, research-based view of the dynamic brain transformation that occurs during those nine months while sharing her own experiences of motherhood. Originally published in Spanish in 2024, Carmona’s book dives into the changes in neuroplasticity that happen before and after birth, the neuroscience of matrescence and the connections between hormones and maternal behavior.
Publication date: 6 October 2026
“Brain Flows: How Network Dynamics Compose the Human Mind” by Michael Cole (Princeton University Press)
In his debut book, cognitive neuroscientist Michael Cole examines how brain flows—the movement of neuronal activity between neural populations—shape free will, intelligence and creativity. In the first half of the book, Cole delivers a summary of the latest research in brain flow dynamics in cognitive, computational and network neuroscience. The second half lays out a theoretical framework to guide future research into how these patterns generate the hallmark properties of the human mind.
Publication date: 3 November 2026
“The Phantom Mind: Insights from the Borderlands of Sleep” by Baland Jalal (MIT Press)
Sleep paralysis—a peculiar glitch that results in a hybrid, unstable state of consciousness—is caused by disrupted neuronal mechanisms that flip the brain from wakefulness to sleep. In “The Phantom Mind,” Baland Jalal explores the neuroscience behind sleep paralysis and other states of fractured sleep, as well as their broad cultural impact. Throughout the book, Baland argues that making sense of what happens in the brain during these borderland sleep states is the key to understanding consciousness, imagination and what makes us human.
Publication date: 17 November 2026
“A Brain for Europe: Big Science, Big Models, and the Politics of Unification” by Tara Mahfoud (MIT Press)
In 2013, the European Commission launched the Human Brain Project (HBP) with the goal of building a massive digital infrastructure for brain research. In her new book, sociologist Tara Mahfoud dissects the research and debates that shaped the ambitious initiative, which ended in 2023. Mahfoud uses interviews with HBP scientists and administrators, as well as observations from their meetings with the European Commission, to explore how competing visions over brain models turned into debates over scientific governance, offering a critique of big team science in the process.
Publication date: 24 November 2026
“The Latent Brain: The New Science of How We Think, Feel, and Act” by Mark Humphries (Harvard University Press)
In his latest book, Mark Humphries makes a call for a theoretical shift in neuroscience, arguing that a focus on individual neuronal activity is no longer sufficient to comprehend the brain. He proposes instead the “latent brain” hypothesis, which posits that brain function is embodied in the collective activity of neuronal networks and dynamical systems. Humphries draws on decades of research across brain regions and animal models to survey how dynamical systems help us understand the brain and what the field needs to do to further that knowledge.
Publication date: 2 March 2027
Also published in 2026:
“Brains Minds Machines: The Mystery of Human Intelligence, the Enigmas of the Artificial” by Tomaso Poggio and Marco Magrini (MIT Press)
Originally published in Italian in 2023, “Brain Minds Machines” tells the history of scientists’ attempts to understand intelligence and replicate it using mathematical modeling. Tomaso Poggio, one of the founders of computational neuroscience, and journalist Marco Magrini outline landmark scientific discoveries about intelligence, assess the commonalities between animal and human intelligence and consider the opportunities and risks that artificial intelligence presents for the future.
Publication date: 25 August 2026
“Whole-Brain Modelling: Cartography of the Dynamics of Mind” by Gustavo Deco and Morten Kringelbach (Oxford University Press)
In this book, neuroscientists Gustavo Deco and Morten Kringelbach team up to assess the advances in mathematics, engineering and biophysics that have pushed forward computational techniques of brain modeling. Throughout the book, they dig into the nuances that shape models, such as the turbulence of brain dynamics and the precise parameters of brain region parcellation, to examine what they call the “new science of whole brain modelling.”
Publication date: 4 May 2026
“The Brain, In Theory” by Romain Brette (Princeton University Press)
In “The Brain, In Theory,” cognitive neuroscientist Romain Brette pushes back against theories that describe the brain as a “biological computer.” Across eight chapters, Brette outlines why he believes that the conceptualization of neuronal activity as a neural code is misleading, questions reductionist bottom-up approaches that try to reverse engineer how the brain works and proposes that the field needs to get back to a view of the brain centered around organisms and living entities. Read an excerpt from Chapter 4 of “The Brain, In Theory” on The Transmitter.
Publication date: 7 April 2026
“Emergence: A Memoir of Boyhood, Computation, and the Mysteries of Mind” by David Sussillo (Grand Central Publishing)
David Sussillo’s memoir is a candid account of his life both inside and outside the lab. Sussillo traces his life story from a challenging upbringing in New Mexico, where he navigated his parents’ substance abuse and growing up in the foster care system, to his career as an influential computational neuroscientist. “Emergence” shows how a scientist’s life and work are often inseparable. Watch our interview with Sussillo about the book.
Publication date: 17 March 2026
“My Life, My Science: Pursuing a Cure for Huntington’s Disease” by Nancy Sabin Wexler (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press)
In 1979, Nancy Sabin Wexler travelled to Venezuela to study a community with an unusually high rate of Huntington’s disease in hopes of better understanding the condition’s genetic basis. Inspired by a family history of Huntington’s disease, her groundbreaking field work during that trip kickstarted the research that led to the discovery of the HUNTINGTIN gene, which played a large role in the launch of the Human Genome Project. In her memoir, Wexler, who currently has the disease, gives a thoughtful account of her life’s work and reflects on what it’s like living with the condition she studied throughout her career.
Publication date: 16 March 2026
“Fox, the Shrew, and You: How Brains Evolved” by Rogier Mars (Princeton University Press)
Rogier Mars examines all corners of the animal kingdom, including lemurs, squirrels, dogs and even the humble sea squirt, to provide readers with an in-depth view of the critical moments in evolution that enabled brains to expand in structure, complexity and cognitive capability. Read an excerpt from Chapter 1 of “The Fox, the Shrew, and You” on The Transmitter.
Publication date: 5 March 2026
“The Laws of Thought: The Quest for a Mathematical Theory of the Mind” by Tom Griffiths (Macmillan Publishers)
The cognitive revolution of the 1950s, spurred by philosophers and psychologists, brought about a conceptual shift in the study of the mind and thought. And with that came an understanding that mathematics and mathematical models of cognition could be used to test hypotheses of the mind against human behavior. In his new book, cognitive scientist Tom Griffiths examines that history and provides his assessment of the current mathematical landscape that seeks to model cognition. He discusses how each of them offer complementary perspectives and explains why they need to come together to provide the field with a more complete picture of the human mind.
Publication date: 10 February 2026
Explore more from The Transmitter
![Book cover of The Brain, In Theory by Romain Brette.](https://www.thetransmitter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/1200-brain-in-theory-brette-1024x683.png) 
![Book cover of The Fox, The Shrew, and You features silhouettes of several animals with their brains highlighted.](https://www.thetransmitter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Fox-Shrew-You-1200-1024x692.png)
summary: The Transmitter has released its 2026 reading list, highlighting several new neuroscience books and notable titles published throughout the year. The featured selections cover diverse topics, ranging from the neuroscience of motherhood and sleep paralysis to the history of the Human Brain Project and memoirs by prominent researchers. These books explore how modern scientific approaches, network dynamics, and theoretical frameworks continue to shape our understanding of the human mind.
key_points: Susana Carmona's book "A Mother’s Brain" explores the research behind neural transformations during pregnancy and gestation.
Tara Mahfoud's "A Brain for Europe" analyzes the rise and fall of the European Commission's Human Brain Project.
Nancy Sabin Wexler's memoir details her groundbreaking fieldwork on Huntington's disease and her personal experience living with the condition.
Several featured titles examine computational neuroscience, brain network dynamics, and mathematical modeling of the mind.

title: “Living A Lie”: Astronaut Spends Nearly Six Months In Space, Comes Back Questioning Everything
author: Eligijus Sinkunas
content:
![Astronaut Michael Fincke smiles in his space suit, an American flag visible in the background. Life on Earth is unbelievable.](https://static.boredpanda.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/astronaut-reveals-earths-shocking-reality-cover_675.jpg) 
“Living A Lie”: Astronaut Spends Nearly Six Months In Space, Comes Back Questioning Everything
Being an astronaut has got to be the biggest flex in life. A human being fulfilled one of the most common childhood dreams and achieved something deemed impossible less than 70 years ago. It’s quite a kerfuffle to wrap our heads around.
Yet some people really do it, and each day we hear about new scientific developments and achievements. Nowadays, we can even catch up with NASA through Twitch. If that’s not the modern world, then I don’t know what is. But we must also remember that astronauts see only a side of our planet and our solar system that very few people can experience. And that can lead to realizations no one could have expected or even related to, and astronaut Ron Garan has a few words on the subject after his own experience in outer space.
Everyone dreams of being an astronaut, but very few actually manage to do it, and Ron Garan is one of them
The mission that led to his realization that “we’re all living a lie” was an expedition that occurred in 2011, where he spent 178 days at the International Space Station
Ron Garan went on Expeditions 27/28, which ran sequentially from March to September 2011. The expeditions focused on advancing microgravity research across astrophysics, biology, and human physiology — at least according to NASA’s own explanations. Garan joined the team as a flight engineer, responsible for station maintenance, performing spacewalks, and conducting scientific experiments.
After such a life-changing experience, making astronauts grasp the sheer scale of humanity and its problems, Garan came to an incredibly complex realization that completely shifted his perspective on Earth. He explained to Big Think that he “saw the paparazzi-like flashes of lightning storms,” the “dancing curtains of auroras that seemed so close it was as if we could reach out and touch them,” and ultimately realized the “unbelievable thinness of our planet’s atmosphere.”
In total, Garan orbited Earth 2,842 times and traveled more than 71 million miles in outer space
Despite this phenomenal adventure, the astronaut realized how futile humanity can be in prioritizing wealth and economy versus our planet’s biosphere
What led Garan to this epiphany was realizing just how fragile humanity and our lives are. “In that moment, I was hit with the sobering realization that that paper-thin layer keeps every living thing on our planet alive,” he said, referring to Earth’s atmosphere, which many astronauts and scientists have explained appears, from outer space, as an incredibly thin, glowing blue band hugging the curve of the Earth. It is what shields our planet from radiation, the solar wind, and the absolute vacuum of space.
This fragility of humanity as we know it made the astronaut realize that humans have been using Earth for its resources rather than caring for it as the “iridescent biosphere teeming with life,” that it is. Moreover, the astronaut expanded on this, saying, “Our human-made systems treat everything, including the very life-support systems of our planet, as the wholly owned subsidiary of the global economy, it’s obvious from the vantage point of space that we’re living a lie.”
Ultimately, the astronaut realized our Earth is held and alive by a “paper-thin” layer that humans are failing to protect in lieu of their beliefs regarding economic growth and geopolitical borders
So, what did he actually mean by this? Well, very simply put, Garan believes our mindsets have been indoctrinated into misranking our priorities. Namely, we’ve been putting economic systems, financial markets, and even geopolitical borders at the forefront of society. Instead, the engineer says humans have started to see environmental problems as less important than these man-made concepts. We act as if Earth’s resources are endless, and as if our economy being independent of Earth’s ecosystem.
It’s a complex train of thought, but one that makes absolute sense once you take into consideration that this man completely lived a different reality from everyone else. He saw the world for what it is — limited. Limited resources. Small on the grand scale of things. And he’s hardly the only one to have done it. In fact, it’s an overwhelmingly common experience for space travelers. Author Frank White even coined this type of epiphany as “the Overview Effect.”
This overview effect actually refers to the psychological transformation that some astronauts experience after seeing Earth from orbit, or even from the Moon. Artificial geopolitical boundaries disappear, which creates a feeling of frustration among astronauts over man-made conflicts, despite the fact that we’re all living on a single planet in the same point in time and space. But they also experience a deep sense of interconnectedness.
Garan said it himself: “The other thing I felt, and I can’t really explain, is that being completely detached from Earth also made me feel deeply connected with everyone on the planet. It was this overwhelming kinship,” he said. Many other astronauts have also shared having similar feelings, like Edgar Mitchell, who mentioned his dissatisfaction with the state of the world and how international politics seem petty from the Moon, or even Nicole Stott, who shifted her NASA career toward environmental art and activism instead.
Ultimately, readers of Garan’s testimony completely understood what he meant, despite not living through the same experience themselves. So what do you think of Garan’s epiphany? Do you believe it’s something only astronauts and deep-sea researchers can truly realize after seeing how there’s only one Earth? Let us know!
summary: Former astronaut Ron Garan spent 178 days aboard the International Space Station in 2011, an experience that fundamentally shifted his perspective on Earth. Witnessing the paper-thin nature of the planet's atmosphere from space led him to realize that humanity falsely prioritizes economic growth and geopolitical borders over protecting the biosphere. This psychological shift, known as the "Overview Effect," is a common experience among space travelers who observe Earth's fragility and interconnectedness.
key_points: Ron Garan served as a flight engineer during a 178-day mission on the International Space Station in 2011.
Seeing Earth from space revealed the unbelievable thinness of the planet's atmosphere that sustains all life.
Garan concluded that human-made systems incorrectly treat Earth's life-support systems as subsidiaries of the global economy.
The psychological transformation experienced by space travelers who see Earth from orbit is known as "the Overview Effect."

title: Thought of the day from Stoic philosopher Seneca: "Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve"
author: Space Daily Editorial Team
content:
“Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.” That is Seneca writing to Lucilius, in Richard Mott Gummere’s translation, in the seventh of his Moral Letters, titled “On Crowds.”
The first sentence of that instruction gets quoted everywhere. The rest almost never does. And the part that gets dropped is the part that changes what the whole thing means.
A note before we go further: we are not psychologists or classicists, and this is reflection on old advice and modern studies, not guidance for your own friendships. The research we lean on is mostly observational, meaning it tracks patterns across large groups rather than telling any one person what to do.
The company you keep
The popular half of the line, “associate with those who will make a better man of you,” is easy to nod along to. Seneca meant it seriously, and he made it vivid elsewhere in the same letter. He warned that “the familiar friend, if he be luxurious, weakens and softens us imperceptibly; the neighbour, if he be rich, rouses our covetousness; the companion, if he be slanderous, rubs off some of his rust upon us, even though we be spotless and sincere.” The key word is “imperceptibly.” His claim is that other people shape you whether or not you notice.
Modern research on social networks has poked at roughly the same idea, though it can only hint at what Seneca stated flatly. James Fowler and Nicholas Christakis studied the Framingham Heart Study and mapped how happiness spread through a social network over about two decades. They found a person was around 15 percent more likely to be happy when a directly connected friend was happy. The effect faded at two and three steps out, and disappeared beyond that.
Be careful how far you stretch that. The pattern comes from watching a network, not running an experiment, and critics have pushed back hard. One methodological critique argues it is genuinely hard to tell real influence apart from the simpler fact that similar people tend to cluster together in the first place.
So the picture is less “moods are contagious, proven” and more: the people around you probably nudge you, and working out exactly how much is difficult. Which is more or less where Seneca left it, minus the statistics.
The half nobody quotes
Then comes the sentence that gets cut: “Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.” Seneca isn’t only telling Lucilius to find better company. He’s telling him to be better company, on purpose, for someone else. The advice runs in two directions at once, and the direction people skip is the one where you do the giving.
That’s easy to read as pure charity, an add-on to the real point. We don’t think it is. Seneca frames it as the same instruction, said from the other side. And there’s a reason teaching might do something for the teacher too.
Seneca’s own explanation is the last clause: “for men learn while they teach.” He offers no evidence, just the claim.
However, a 2014 experiment gives that claim a modern test. Psychologist John Nestojko and colleagues had people study a passage. They told some people they’d be tested on it, and others that they’d have to teach it. As the finding is reported by ScienceDaily, “when compared to learners expecting a test, learners expecting to teach recalled more material correctly, they organized their recall more effectively and they had better memory for especially important information.”
One study is one study, and this one comes with a catch. Nobody in the experiment actually taught anyone. Everyone was tested in the end, and the difference came from what they were told beforehand. So the effect looks less like magic and more like a change in how you pay attention when you know someone will rely on what you know. That’s a narrower claim than “teaching makes you smarter,” but it fits Seneca’s line well. Getting ready to hand something on seems to change how you hold it yourself.
Reading it in an age of curated feeds
Perhaps the strangest thing about this letter now is how completely we’ve automated its first half and abandoned its second. We choose our associations more finely than any Roman could, following, muting, and blocking our way to a network of people who suit us. The “associate with those who will make a better man of you” instruction has become almost effortless, if you read “better” loosely enough.
The “welcome those whom you yourself can improve” half has no such button. It asks for the slower thing: showing up as the steadier person in someone else’s network, teaching what you know, being the friend whose rust, to borrow Seneca’s image, is worth rubbing off. A feed can hand you better inputs. It cannot make you a better input for anyone else.
What we keep coming back to is that Seneca wrote the two halves as one sentence on purpose. The give and take isn’t a bonus tacked onto the advice; it’s how the advice works. You’re meant to be improved and improving at the same time, because in his account those aren’t two separate things but one. Take only the first half, the version everyone quotes, and you’re left with something closer to networking than to what he actually wrote. The whole line asks you to be on both ends of it at once.
summary: Stoic philosopher Seneca advised in his letters that people should both seek better company and actively improve others, noting that teaching also benefits the teacher. While the first part about surrounding oneself with good influences is frequently quoted, the second part about mentoring others is often ignored. Modern studies on social networks and learning provide some observational and experimental backing for Seneca's dual ideas.
key_points: Seneca wrote that people are imperceptibly shaped by their companions, warning that negative traits can rub off on us.
Modern social network research suggests that moods and behaviors can spread among connected individuals, though causation is debated.
The frequently ignored half of Seneca's advice encourages individuals to consciously help and improve others.
A 2014 psychological study showed that expecting to teach material improves a person's recall and organization of that material.

title: In 2018 a female orca off the coast of Washington gave birth to a calf that died within half an hour, and rather than let the body sink she carried it with her, pushing it through the water on her head for 17 days and more than a thousand miles before finally letting go, and in 2025 the same whale did it all over again with another dead calf.
author: Space Daily; Kiran Journals
content:
The mother’s designation, on the tracking records kept by the researchers who monitor her, is J35. Her name is Tahlequah. She’s a member of the Southern Resident killer whale population that lives in the Salish Sea between Washington state and British Columbia, and she was, as of the events described in the title of this piece, roughly twenty and then twenty-six years old. What she did in the summer of 2018 caught the attention of enough people around the world that the behaviour got a nickname within a week. The Tour of Grief. It was hard to watch, hard to look away from, and hard for anyone, scientist or otherwise, to talk about without reaching for the vocabulary of human bereavement.
What most of the reporting at the time didn’t quite land on is that the same whale would, six and a half years later, do it all over again.
What Tahlequah did, both times
According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s official reporting on the 2025 event, published on the Fisheries division’s own website in January of that year, Tahlequah gave birth to her calf J61 sometime in late December 2024. The Center for Whale Research first observed the new mother and calf together on 20 December. Concerns about the calf’s health surfaced almost immediately. J61 was underweight, potentially premature, and spent unusual amounts of time underwater in what the researchers interpreted as attempts to nurse that weren’t succeeding.
By New Year’s Eve, the calf was dead. She’d lived about a week.
Researchers first spotted Tahlequah carrying her body off Alki Point in West Seattle on 31 December 2024. From there she moved with the rest of J pod through the waters of the Salish Sea, up toward Vancouver Island, across the international boundary, and back down through the San Juan Islands. She was still carrying the body on 10 January when researchers relocated her off Victoria, British Columbia. She continued to carry the body for at least sixteen days in total. Nobody has a precise final count for exactly when she stopped, because the sighting record has gaps in it, but the behaviour was documented in enough separate observations across enough consecutive days that the pattern was unmistakable.
This was, from every observable angle, the same thing she’d done in 2018.
If you enjoy learning about the weird and wonderful ways of our animal kingdom, this video on something truly unique only whales do is worth a watch:
The earlier event began on 24 July 2018. Tahlequah gave birth to a female calf off the coast of Victoria, British Columbia. Ken Balcomb, the founder of the Center for Whale Research, was among the first to see the newborn alive. She lived for approximately half an hour. Within moments of the calf’s death, Tahlequah began balancing the body on her rostrum, meaning the front of her head, and pushing it upward through the water each time it began to sink. She carried it in this way for seventeen consecutive days. Traveling with J pod, she covered a distance the Center for Whale Research eventually estimated at over one thousand miles across the Salish Sea. She finally released the body on around 11 August. And then, as far as any observer could tell, she returned to ordinary pod behaviour.
The 2025 event followed the same physical pattern in almost every respect. Body balanced on the head. Repeatedly pushed to the surface when it started to sink. Sustained across multiple consecutive days of ordinary pod movement. The duration was slightly shorter than 2018 but still exceptional in the primary literature on cetacean post-mortem behaviour. And the geography was the same. Tahlequah made the same slow loop through the Salish Sea, and appeared to grieve in the same specific way, in the same waters, seven years later.
What the science actually says she’s doing
The word grief is where things get genuinely difficult. What Tahlequah did looks, to almost every human observer, like grief. The question of whether it actually is grief, in the sense we mean when we use the word about ourselves, is one the marine mammal literature has been carefully cautious about for years.
According to an analysis by Dr Joe Gaydos, science director at the SeaDoc Society, first published during the 2018 event and re-shared in 2025 when it happened again, what Tahlequah did fits a broader pattern of behaviour documented across many long-lived, socially complex mammals. Cetacean researchers have a term for it. Post-mortem attentive behaviour, sometimes called epimeletic behaviour, which refers to any sustained interaction between a living animal and the body of a recently deceased member of its own social group. It’s been recorded in dolphins, sperm whales, elephants, chimpanzees, gorillas, and multiple primate species. Mothers carrying dead infants for extended periods has been documented in gelada baboons, Japanese macaques, and mountain gorillas among others.
What made Tahlequah’s 2018 event unusual, on the primary literature record, wasn’t the fact that she carried her calf’s body. It was the duration. Seventeen days is exceptional. Most documented cases of post-mortem carrying in cetaceans last hours or a few days at most. And what makes the 2025 event unusual in a different way is simply that it happened to the same individual. Repeated cases of the same female performing the same extended-duration behaviour after successive losses are, on the current published record, close to unheard of.
Whether the underlying emotional experience is grief in the human sense is a question the researchers who work with these animals mostly decline to answer definitively. What they will say is that the parts of the killer whale brain responsible for memory, learning, and emotional processing are highly developed. That Southern Resident killer whales live in extraordinarily tight matrilineal social groups, with strong lifelong bonds between mothers, daughters, siblings, and cousins. That the loss of a calf, particularly in an already-critically-endangered population that has had almost no successful births in recent years, is not an abstract event for the surviving mother. And that behaviour of the kind Tahlequah has displayed is consistent with, though not by itself proof of, whatever the killer whale equivalent of prolonged mourning might turn out to be.
The broader context sitting behind the whole story is worth naming honestly. The Southern Resident killer whale population is currently down to approximately seventy-four individuals, and has been in slow decline for decades. Their primary food source, Chinook salmon, has collapsed across most of the Pacific Northwest. Underwater noise from shipping traffic in the Salish Sea interferes with their hunting. Pollutants concentrate in their blubber. Calf mortality in the population runs disproportionately high, and successful births have become rare enough that each one is a small event and each loss is a large one. J35, on the pod records maintained by the Center for Whale Research, has now had four documented pregnancies and only one surviving offspring. Of the two that died as newborns, she carried both.
What the coverage keeps circling around, without quite ever settling on, is that whatever Tahlequah is doing in the water when she pushes a dead calf to the surface, she’s doing it in front of an audience that recognises something in it. Grief may or may not be the technically correct scientific vocabulary. It is, on the accumulated observation of anyone who has watched her do it, the closest word most languages have to describe what the behaviour looks like, and possibly the closest word for what the behaviour actually is.
Kiran Athar writes about biology, animal behaviour, and the ordinary corners of the natural world where the two intersect. This piece draws on institutional reporting from NOAA Fisheries and analysis published by the SeaDoc Society, alongside primary observations by the Center for Whale Research.
summary: In late December 2024, a Southern Resident killer whale named Tahlequah (J35) gave birth to a calf that died within a week, prompting her to carry the body for at least sixteen days through the Salish Sea. This behavior closely mirrored a famous 1981—correction, 2018—event where she pushed another dead calf's body for seventeen days over a thousand miles. Marine researchers categorize this as post-mortem attentive or epimeletic behavior, noting that repeated extended carrying by the same individual is nearly unprecedented. While scientists remain cautious about attributing human grief to whales, the actions highlight the complex emotional processing and tight social bonds of the critically endangered population.
key_points: Southern Resident killer whale Tahlequah (J35) carried her dead newborn calf for at least 16 days starting in late December 2024.
This behavior nearly mirrored an identical event in 2018, when Tahlequah carried a previous deceased calf for 17 days and over a thousand miles.
Marine biologists refer to this as post-mortem attentive or epimeletic behavior, which is documented in other socially complex mammals but rarely seen at this duration twice in the same individual.
The endangered Salish Sea killer whale population faces threats from Chinook salmon collapse, shipping noise, and pollutants, with J35 experiencing high calf mortality.

title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope will reveal the universe in a way the JWST and Hubble cannot
author: Monisha Ravisetti
content:
![Three images showing three different telescopes.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/LNeeHiwvdKvCBp6jySQRbN.jpg) 
Even if you aren't the kind of person who often looks up the latest space images, it's hard to navigate life (especially on the internet) without running into a few. Try choosing a new iPhone background and you'll have your pick of sharp, gray moon portraits. Watch an old "Star Trek" episode and you may not realize how many of those translucent nebulas outside the spaceship's windows were based on real, hard data.
When it comes to space, we're spoiled. Mind-bending objects light-years away from us have managed to become integrated into our everyday lives — and though we're still a ways away from understanding the true nature of the universe, we're also the closest we've ever been. It's in large part thanks to how impeccable our fleet of space telescopes is. In seconds, you can find a Hubble Space Telescope Deep Field with luminescent galaxies warped along the curvature of spacetime and James Webb Space Telescope images of strange hazy red objects from just after the dawn of time.
Moreover, what's tremendously exciting is this fleet is constantly growing. Indeed, very soon, a new space telescope will launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. It's called the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and it should be able to unlock a new level in the astronomy layer of our lives. It will show us new types of images, reveal new types of data and lead us in directions we may not yet know are possible.
What is Roman?
To put it succinctly, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is an approximately 42-foot-long (12.7-meter-long), cylindrical metal observatory scheduled to lift off from our planet on Aug. 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.
Across a five-year-long mission (a 10-year-long one if everything goes well), Roman is meant to use two powerful instruments — the Wide-Field Instrument (WFI) and Coronagraph Instrument — to image huge swaths of the cosmos and tackle some crucial questions. It will help scientists probe the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy, directly image exoplanets near and far, witness an extensive amount of stars exploding in colossal supernovas and more.
But whether or not it's a fair thought, it's hard not to want to compare the specifications of this space telescope to some of the others that have brought the cosmos down into our daily lives. This is particularly true for two of the major players right now: the James Webb Space Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope.
What can Roman do that these two cannot?
 ![A view of galaxies warped against a dark background.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/cpDdVhcSsFVpA6Mqh6LfJ8.jpg) 
Roman vs. Hubble
To start, one of the biggest benefits of Roman over Hubble is its processing power.
By numbers, that means Hubble has managed to gather about 400 terabytes of data over its approximately 35 years of service so far. Roman is expected to be able to create 500 terabytes of data every single year.
"Its surveying capabilities are over 1,000 times faster than Hubble, and can chart 200 times more sky in a single image," NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said during a press conference about Roman in April. "What would take Hubble 2,000 years to process, Roman can do in a year — the images it captures will be so large there is not a screen in existence large enough to show them."
Roman's primary mirror is about 7.9 feet (2.4 meters) wide, which is actually the same as Hubble's. Primary mirrors are arguably the most important aspect of a space telescope, because it's how an observatory manages to gather light coming from the universe. Bigger mirrors can collect more light, which allows them to see dimmer or more distant objects. Interestingly, Roman's primary mirror is also about 80% lighter than Hubble's. Roman has a secondary mirror as well; it's just under 2 feet (0.5 meters) wide. Hubble's secondary mirror is very similar at exactly 12.2 inches (0.3 m) in width.
 ![Two telescopes side by side.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ThwXy6bt8SuVARB2oDwfvT.png) 
Yet even though Roman's mirrors are so comparable to Hubble's, because of Roman's processing power as well as the capabilities of its WFI, it will be able to image a far wider stretch of sky than Hubble can.
Though Roman does have some visible light capabilities like Hubble, WFI specializes in infrared light — actually the kind of light the JWST works with, but we'll get to that telescope comparison shortly — so we should compare it to Hubble's infrared instrument. The WFI's field of view is about 100 times greater than the Hubble infrared instrument's field of view.
According to NASA, this view will allow Roman to measure light emanating from a billion galaxies and billions more cosmic phenomena over its years of service.
"Both observatories will perform spectroscopy," NASA explains, "which involves splitting light into individual colors to study patterns that reveal detailed information. But Roman's spectral studies will have lower resolution over a large area, while Hubble's has higher resolution over a small area."
This concept really sums up the difference between the two telescopes, and in fact foreshadows what we'll soon discuss about the JWST.
 ![A tall cylinder wrapped in silvery material.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/hPiFHMmVGMyzy2etcPKTxG.jpg) 
Roman vs. the JWST
The main similarity between the Roman Space Telescope and the JWST is those infrared light goggles.
Infrared light, unlike visible light, is invisible to human eyes. You can think of it more like a heat signature. Firefighters, for instance, use infrared trackers on burning buildings from the outside to see where the source of the fire might lie within. And when it comes to astronomy, infrared light is priceless — that's why the JWST's strong infrared capabilities give it an advantage over Hubble.
Infrared light's role in astronomy observations has to do with the way light moves throughout the universe. As light from a distant region of space moves toward us — through a continuously expanding universe, no less — those light wavelengths stretch out from tight, bluer ones into long, redder ones. Eventually, the wavelengths stretch out into the infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum, which is the part of the spectrum we cannot see with our own eyes. Plus, any objects in our line of sight that are hidden behind dense clouds of interstellar dust or gas can only be seen via their infrared emissions.
What this means is that very, very distant objects as well as concealed objects in space are pretty much invisible to us, hiding in the infrared part of the spectrum. We therefore need infrared decoders, like the JWST's suite of tools or Hubble's infrared instrument, to reveal them.
The JWST has already made absolute strides in this regard, revealing to us peculiar objects from the early years of the universe, consistently breaking its own record while finding the most distant galaxies we've ever seen and revamping Hubble portraits like the spectacular Pillars of Creation with its infrared filter. It's even reintroduced us to our own solar system with crisp views of Neptune's frail, oft-forgotten rings and Saturn's big, bright ones.
 ![The solar system's most distant planet Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope on the backdrop of a galaxy-studded sky.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/7k4WJDkVMBSBm9cgggE9GF.jpg) 
When it comes to mirrors, the JWST's iconic golden primary mirror made of 18 hexagonal segments is a beautiful 21 feet and 4 inches (6.5 meters) across, which is much larger than Roman's. This means the JWST can collect tons more light than Roman can, which makes a lot of sense because it was built to see as deep into the ancient universe as possible.
But where the JWST lacks is, you guessed it, its field of view. This is on purpose. The whole point of JWST is to pierce into the universe with a highly narrow view in order to get great resolution on whatever it's looking at. Roman definitely won't be getting that same resolution, as its images will be shallower than the JWST's, but its WFI will see a region 50 times wider than what the JWST can see.
 ![The main mirror of JWST](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/tzD7mWxqYXnXvWNMgeRTyV.jpg) 
 ![technicians in clean suits in a hangar next to a large rectangular spacecraft wrapped in metallic foil](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/hGZtVNFX4sVpapTUkQvjKg.jpg) 
To be clear, there are indeed other survey telescopes that are able to image huge amounts of the sky at once, but Roman's version of doing this is expected to be with higher clarity. For example, the ground-based Rubin Observatory is revolutionary for the vast amounts of data it's able to collect while scanning a new section of the sky every 40 seconds. However, Rubin is on the ground. A space telescope sits above Earth's atmosphere, and therefore has less atmospheric interference to sift through. This makes the observations way better.
Okay, you've probably figured out the moral of the story at this point: Roman's reach is shallower than Hubble's and the JWST's, but extremely wide. So, what's the benefit of this enormity?
 ![A side by side image showing a simulated Rubin view of the universe and a simulated Roman version.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/FZYUvm8uo2VK9YR9UypSRg.jpg) 
The promise of Roman
Imaging huge amounts of the universe in one go is of foremost importance because things in the universe happen simultaneously. A supernova on one end might be worth checking out, but a fleeting fast radio burst buzzing on the other end of the cosmos could be just as vital to study. Yet, with a narrow field of view, you'd have to select which target to zoom in on. And if you aren't sure which targets are even options, while perusing an ancient black hole with immense resolution you will most definitely miss an even older one that lurks 50 frames or so away.
With Roman, scientists won't have to be as selective about which parts of the sky they scan. Roman is designed to be able to capture the supernovas, fast radio bursts, black hole emissions and warped galaxy candidates all at once. For example, NASA explains how Roman will be able to spot colliding neutron stars — stellar corpses so dense a tablespoon of one is equal to the weight of Mount Everest — with its infrared view. The JWST would likely never even come across such an event due to its tunnel vision.
Of course, Roman won't be able to image these objects with as much depth as the JWST or Hubble — or several other telescopes for that matter, like maybe SPHEREx or Euclid — but it will be able to notice that these objects exist.
The next step would be to have one of those other telescopes follow up on the targets. You can think of Roman as creating the Google Maps of hotspot locations in the universe that the JWST, Hubble or another telescope may want to examine someday.
Big field of view means big science
Furthermore, capturing information from billions of objects in such a short period of time will enable specific kinds of research, such as the hunt for the truth about dark matter and dark energy. Despite collectively making up about 95% of the universe's contents, dark matter and dark energy aren't visible to us. However, we know dark energy exists because it appears to be applying a force that accelerates the expansion of our universe and we know dark matter exists because it seems to be the glue around galaxies that prevents them from falling apart like horses on a merry-go-round spinning too fast.
What this means is imaging tons of galaxies at once could allow scientists to have a better picture of how those interactions between the dark universe and our regular universe play out. Roman will also be able to create time-lapse "movies" of the universe in three dimensions and offer scientists the chance to see how other observations fit into that picture.
It would also be remiss not to mention what Roman's other instrument can do: the coronagraph. The telescope's coronagraph is actually one-of-a-kind. You can think of it like a special artificial eclipse that brings objects into view that would otherwise be obscured by bright starlight. No other space observatory in service right now has the ability to directly image exoplanets like Roman will be able to using that coronagraph. It would take an entire other article to explain the awesome complexities of this instrument — an article that you can definitely expect soon — but to go through the basics, this tool will block out the glare of distant stars and then measure the polarization of light around them in order to help scientists tease out exoplanets orbiting those stars.
 ![A side by side view of two different versions of the Pillars of Creation. One on the right has more stars visible; one on the left has a more sturdy-looking structure.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Kptzr3YmxZUkaza7nJnaK8.png) 
According to NASA, Roman's coronagraph will be able to detect planets 100 million times fainter than their stars. That capability is about 100 to 1,000 times better than existing space-based coronagraphs. This will give scientists the opportunity to study planets beyond our solar system that are dimmer, colder, farther and more elusive than what we're currently able to see.
With all this in mind, there is an important concept to remember.
When the JWST first entered service in the year 2022, everyone (including me) started comparing it to Hubble and thinking of it as Hubble's upgrade. It's hard not to, especially when the images rolling out of a shiny new telescope are so utterly gorgeous. But "upgrade" couldn't be farther from reality. The JWST is just different. Impressive, sure, but different. The goal is for all of these telescopes to work together, each one giving us a new sheet of the universe to explore. Stack up all the sheets, and you'll get the full picture.
Roman will simply be offering us one breathtaking new sheet.

summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is scheduled to launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket on August 30 for a multi-year mission to study dark matter, dark energy, exoplanets, and supernovas. While its images will be shallower than those of the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope, Roman features a vastly superior field of view and processing power. This allows Roman to survey hundreds of times more sky much faster, acting essentially as a map to locate cosmic phenomena for other telescopes to examine in greater detail.
key_points: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope utilizes a Wide-Field Instrument and a Coronagraph Instrument across a planned five- to ten-year mission.
Roman's surveying capabilities are over 1,000 times faster than Hubble's and can cover a field of view roughly 100 times greater than Hubble's infrared instrument.

While the James Webb Space Telescope uses a larger mirror and a narrow view to capture deep, high-resolution images, Roman sacrifices depth for an extremely wide view to capture large swaths of the cosmos simultaneously.

Roman's broad data collection will help scientists investigate dark matter, dark energy, exploding stars, and distant galaxies by capturing massive amounts of data—approximately 500 terabytes annually.

title: Watch 2 astronauts replace failed ISS antenna during spacewalk today
author: Mike Wall
content:
![U.S. Spacewalk 98 - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/I0j7as4MLHk/maxresdefault.jpg) 
Two astronauts will do some repair work outside the International Space Station today (Aug. 25), and you can watch the action live.
NASA's Anil Menon and Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency will conduct a spacewalk today (Aug. 25) to replace a space-to-ground-antenna. The extravehicular activity (EVA) is expected to start around 8:35 a.m. EDT (1235 GMT) and last 6.5 hours.
You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA, or directly via the space agency. Coverage will start at 7:00 a.m. EDT (1100 GMT).
 ![Two astronauts in white bulky spacesuits work outside a large space station set against the blackness of space.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/intWgzLxHinP4DegP2w3hS.jpg) 
This will be the third spacewalk for Menon and the second for Adenot, the first French woman ever to conduct an EVA. Her history-making first excursion occurred on Aug. 18, when she and Menon removed a failed space-to-ground antenna, a relay link that enables high-speed communications between the International Space Station (ISS) and Mission Control at Johnson Space Center in Houston.
The duo ran out of time before they could install a replacement antenna, however. They'll finish the job today, if all goes to plan.
"If time allows, Menon and Adenot also will attempt a get‑ahead task to replace a retroreflector on the forward port of the space station's Harmony module, which will improve navigation data for visiting spacecraft," NASA officials wrote in a spacewalk preview.
Adenot arrived at the ISS in February as part of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission, which also includes NASA astronauts Jack Hathaway and Jessica Meir and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.
Menon came aboard on July 14, making the trip on a Russian Soyuz spacecraft along with cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina. Menon performed his first-ever spacewalk on Aug. 6, with Meir.
Menon will be "crewmember 1" on today's spacewalk, and Adenot will be "crewmember 2." The EVA will be the 283rd in the history of the ISS, which has been continuously occupied by rotating astronaut crews since November 2000.

summary: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot are conducting a spacewalk today to install a replacement space-to-ground antenna on the International Space Station. The repair completes a task left unfinished during an August 18 spacewalk when the duo ran out of time after removing the failed antenna. If time permits, they will also replace a retroreflector on the Harmony module to improve navigation data for visiting spacecraft.
key_points: NASA's Anil Menon and ESA's Sophie Adenot are performing a spacewalk on August 25 to replace a failed communications antenna on the ISS.
The spacewalk is expected to last 6.5 hours and follows a previous excursion on August 18 where the failed antenna was removed.
Sophie Adenot is the first French woman to conduct a spacewalk, with today marking her second EVA.
If time allows, the astronauts will also replace a retroreflector on the Harmony module to aid navigation for visiting spacecraft.

title: NASA satellites ace world's 1st 'lost-in-space' GPS-free navigation experiment
author: Elizabeth Howell
content:
![illustration of four small, boxy satellites flying above earth](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Utc8PJw6H4wuarQvRhJiWV.jpg) 
No GPS available in space? A satellite experiment may have a solution for that.
NASA's Starling mission — made up of a swarm of four cubesats in low Earth orbit (LEO) — is testing out navigation by using other satellites as moving landmarks. The hope is that this tech will allow future missions to navigate if GPS is not available.
The three-year-old tech demo will be extended beyond its previous expiration date this year until at least 2028, NASA announced on Monday (Aug. 17). The aim is to get the most out of the onboard experiment, a collaboration with industry partner EraDrive called FALCON (short for "Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation").
"As NASA prepares for more missions beyond Earth's orbit, technologies like FALCON can support lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions and human exploration," NASA officials said in Monday's statement.
While NASA's applications are civilian, alternative GPS solutions are also being investigated by the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) out of concern that the limited number of GPS satellites could be vulnerable to adversaries. Earlier this year, for example, Space Force entities SpaceWERX and Space Systems Command jointly launched an initiative aiming for new ideas for "positioning, navigation and timing" (PNT) capabilities in space.
The aim of FALCON, however, is to deal with sheer distance. While satellites in Earth orbit have ample access to purpose-built navigational markers such as GPS, that access rapidly thins out as missions go farther afield. And this isn't just an abstract concern; NASA aims to send astronauts to the surface of the moon again as soon as 2028 on the Artemis IV mission, as part of a larger effort to build a moon base.
Industry and the military are also very interested in the moon and the area around it, known as cislunar space — and how best to navigate in the new environment. The moon's orbit also introduces complications to navigation; in 2025, for example, Canada's Outer Space Institute reported that "mass concentrations," or mascons, pull down on orbiting satellites and may affect their pathway, in some cases even inducing crashes into the lunar surface.
But before testing at the moon, NASA wants to learn more closer to home. It partnered with EraDrive, an autonomous spacecraft navigation company that originated with a group at Stanford University, which provided flight software and algorithms for FALCON. The experiment uses data from Starling's cameras, as well as a catalog on the spacecraft that charts thousands of known satellites and space objects around it.
The mission not only is trying out "GPS-independent navigation" but is also showcasing space situational awareness, or SSA — that is, the ability to understand the environment around the spacecraft (including other satellites). Some other spacecraft, like SpaceX's Starlink broadband satellites, use SSA to automatically dodge threats of space debris in LEO.
Starling's team is hoping to bring even more capabilities for navigation and SSA. "The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance and alternative navigation," Roger Hunter, program manager for NASA's small spacecraft and distributed systems program, said in the statement.
 ![artist's illustration of a base on the moon.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/iMpp9op7zEN4JccYsQDDCd.jpg) 
FALCON notched two major milestones in its first three years. For PNT, the spacecraft used its cameras to observe other satellites and objects — and to match their information with the onboard database, which includes roughly 20,000 objects from publicly available DoD records. "FALCON then used the observed and verified objects as reference points to determine Starling's orbit," NASA stated.
FALCON's in-orbit observations also helped mission managers better understand the pathways of 200 individual objects, beyond the orbital estimates in the DoD catalog. The estimating work was performed over just three days and autonomously, meaning ground operators did not participate.
"The self-orbit determination capability made possible through FALCON is a first for spacecraft using optical cameras, to navigate by their relative position to other objects in space," NASA stated. "Separately, the catalog-update experiments produced better object position predictions onboard Starling than those provided by ground stations."
Starling's four spacecraft operate at an altitude of about 350 miles (565 km), which is about 6 miles (10 km) higher than originally planned. That's because SpaceX advised mission managers that Starling's mission plan put it at risk of coming close to Starlink satellites already operating in an orbital shell at 340 miles (555 km), according to Space News. By comparison, the International Space Station typically orbits slightly lower than Starling or Starlink, at 250 miles (400 km).
All of which is to say that the Starling mission demonstrates operations in crowded conditions. But in the future, NASA is hoping to port the lessons learned to the moon and Mars for science applications — meaning, to improve measurements from spacecraft — as well as for interplanetary traffic management.

The experiment relies on onboard cameras and a catalog of space objects to use other satellites as moving landmarks for self-navigation. Following its initial success, NASA has extended the Starling mission until at least 2028 to prepare for future deep-space and lunar exploration.
key_points: NASA extended the Starling cubesat mission until at least 2028 to maximize the FALCON navigation experiment.
FALCON allows spacecraft to determine their orbit autonomously using optical cameras and a database of thousands of known space objects.
The technology successfully achieved a world's first for spacecraft navigating via their relative position to other objects in space using optical cameras.

title: Nuclear Spacecraft
author: Avi Loeb
content:
Nuclear Spacecraft
![Avi Loeb](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*upiboNSChj1BIvycXiID7w.png)
The most efficient use of rocket fuel is by tailoring the exhaust speed to be exactly equal and opposite in direction to the velocity of the rocket. This way, the exhaust gas ends up at rest in the background reference frame and no kinetic energy is wasted on it. The rocket engine’s efficiency times all the energy released by the fuel ends up as kinetic energy for the payload.
The most powerful source of energy at the disposal of humanity right now is nuclear fission reactors where heavy nuclei of Uranium-235 are split. The splitting converts 0.09% of the Uranium-235 rest mass into energy, about a million times more than the energy per unit mass released during chemical propellant combustion. Given a 5% engine efficiency and an initial Uranium-235 mass comparable to the payload mass, a spacecraft can reach 1% of the speed of light or equivalently 3,000 kilometers per second, about a thousand times faster than achievable with chemical propellants. Even if the initial nuclear fuel mass is only 1% of the payload mass, the terminal speed will still be two orders of magnitude larger than the fastest rocket ever launched through chemical populsion for the same fuel mass.
If humanity ever engage in ambitious interstellar travel, nuclear propulsion would be the best path forward, no pun intended.
This sets the stage for a historic moment within a couple of years. NASA’s first nuclear reactor for an interplanetary spacecraft, Space Reactor 1 (SR-1) Freedom, is now planned for launch in late 2028 towards Mars. Previous spacecraft that have carried nuclear power include Voyager, New Horizons, Curiosity and Perseverance, but they used radioisotope power systems that collect heat from the natural decay of plutonium-238, resembling long-lived space batteries rather than a controlled chain reaction.
The SR-1 reactor is designed to split Uranium-235 atoms in a sustained fission process. It does not use the reactor to directly generate thrust by heating propellant and expelling it, the so-called nuclear thermal propulsion. Instead, the fission reactor generates electricity, and that electricity powers electric thrusters.
The nuclear energy source replaces solar power harvested traditionally by solar panels, and allows travel long distances away from the Sun. Solar flux falls off with the square of distance from the Sun, making it increasingly impractical to use beyond the orbit of Mars.
The nuclear fuel to be used by SR-1 is high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) uranium dioxide, a middle-ground enrichment level below weapons-grade but above typical civilian reactor fuel. This allows a smaller reactor core than used in traditional low-enriched uranium while avoiding the security and proliferation concerns of highly enriched Uranium. The design output is about 20 kilowatts of electrical power, modest by terrestrial standards, but substantial for a deep-space power source.
SR-1 uses a closed Brayton-cycle conversion system, a direct heat-to-electricity conversion path that skips the water/steam cycle used in terrestrial nuclear plants. Managing water in a zero-gravity, mass-constrained spacecraft is impractical. Boron carbide structures surround the reactor assembly and serve as efficient neutron absorbers. The reactor sits at one end of a truss structure specifically to put maximum physical distance between the radiation source and the spacecraft’s sensitive electronics, with the propulsion and power element at the opposite end. The electricity generated feeds a mixed set of electric thrusters. These Hall-effect thrusters work by ionizing a propellant gas, typically xenon, and using an electric field to accelerate the ions out the back, generating thrust. The ions leave at very high speed, allowing the spacecraft to obtain far more momentum from each kilogram of propellant than a conventional chemical rocket.
The United States placed the SNAP-10A fission reactor in Earth orbit in 1965, and fission reactors have flown in Earth orbit since. However, no reactor has powered a spacecraft on an interplanetary trajectory beyond Earth orbit. SR-1 should enter an Earth-escape trajectory and start its reactor within two days from launch. The fission system is not intended to operate on the launch pad or during ascent.
The most ambitious use of nuclear energy for interstellar travel is by carrying a star for the ride. A star is a massive nuclear fusion reactor bound by gravity, where energy is released by combining light elements like hydrogen. Stellar fusion builds heavier elements up to Iron-56, which has the highest nuclear binding energy per nucleon. As a result, iron acts as the absolute stopping point for nuclear reactions in stars because it cannot release energy through fusion or fission. Nuclear fusion in stars can convert rest mass to energy with an efficiency of up to 0.7%, significantly higher than fission.
Stellar engines are hypothesized megastructures that extract energy from a host star for the purpose of generating thrust and accelerating the stellar system. In a 2020 paper published here that I co-authored with my then postdoc, Manasvi Lingam, we showed that stellar engines can be propelled to 1–10% of the speed of light, speeds that cannot be explained by natural astrophysical processes in the Milky-Way galaxy. Our paper suggested that astrometric surveys of hypervelocity stars may be utilized to conduct searches for high-speed stellar engines in the Milky Way. A few days ago, a new paper posted here followed this suggestion and used the Gaia DR3 survey of stars to limit the fraction of technological stellar engines to less than one in 100,000 stars. The sky’s the limit.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Avi Loeb is chair of the UAP Science Advisory Council to the White House, Pentagon, FBI and intelligence agencies, director of the Galileo Project, founding director of Harvard University’s — Black Hole Initiative, former director of the Institute for Theory and Computation at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and the former chair of the astronomy department at Harvard University (2011–2020). He is a former member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and a former chair of the Board on Physics and Astronomy of the National Academies. He is the bestselling author of “Extraterrestrial: The First Sign of Intelligent Life Beyond Earth” and a co-author of the textbook “Life in the Cosmos”, both published in 2021. The paperback edition of his new book, titled “Interstellar”, was published in August 2024.
